rows.statement: Experiment 5: formal Architecture Board approval evidences Authority-authorizes->Decision, conditional on the approval record being evidenced; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.13 — Authority scope ... AuthorityScope. An Architecture Board may have authority over Architecture. It may not automatically have authority over ProductionOperations.
rows.statement: States AuthorityScope must be checked separately: architecture authority does not automatically extend to production operations authority.

rows.anchor: 117.14 — Experiment 6 ... Architecture Board approves target architecture. Operations team performs production deployment. Expected: these are potentially two separate authority boundaries. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: architecture approval and production deployment execution are potentially two separate authority boundaries; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.15 — Stage 4: Implementation ... Decision→Implementation. Decision→ADR→Commit→BuildArtifact.
rows.statement: Defines the Decision->Implementation stage via Decision->ADR->Commit->BuildArtifact.

rows.anchor: 117.16 — Experiment 7 ... Decision says containerize Nexus. Git contains a commit introducing Containerfile, Podman configuration, deployment configuration. Expected: potential implementation evidence. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: a commit introducing containerization artifacts matching a decision is potential implementation evidence; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.17 — Strong implementation relationship ... commit references decision; PR references ADR; implementation record references change request; deployment references build artifact. Then Decision-implementedBy->Change.
rows.statement: Defines strong Decision-implementedBy->Change evidence via explicit cross-references between commit/PR/implementation-record/deployment and decision/ADR/change-request/build-artifact.

rows.anchor: 117.18 — Experiment 8 ... Commit message explicitly references the approved change. Expected: ImplementationTrace=Strong. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: a commit explicitly referencing the approved change yields ImplementationTrace=Strong; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.19 — Stage 5: Verification ... Implementation→Verification. unit tests, integration tests, architecture tests, security tests, deployment checks, smoke tests, operational validation.
rows.statement: Defines Implementation->Verification across seven possible verification types.

rows.anchor: 117.20 — Experiment 9 ... Container starts successfully. Does that prove the architecture is correct? No. It proves RuntimeStartup=True. Not ArchitectureConformance=True. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: a successfully starting container proves RuntimeStartup=True, not ArchitectureConformance=True; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.21 — Verification dimensions ... FunctionalVerification, ArchitectureVerification, SecurityVerification, OperationalVerification. One successful test cannot represent all four.
rows.statement: Separates verification into four dimensions (Functional/Architecture/Security/Operational), stating one test cannot represent all four.

rows.anchor: 117.22 — Experiment 10 ... Nexus container responds on port 8081. Expected: OperationalVerification. But not necessarily ArchitectureVerification. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: a responding container evidences OperationalVerification but not necessarily ArchitectureVerification; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.23 — Deterministic assurance ... Rule→DeterministicCheck→Result. NoForbiddenDependency can be mechanically tested.
rows.statement: Connects to the deterministic-assurance principle Rule->DeterministicCheck->Result, illustrated by mechanically testable NoForbiddenDependency.

rows.anchor: 117.24 — Experiment 11 ... Architecture rule says service must not access production database directly. A static architecture test proves the dependency graph complies. Expected: VerificationEvidence. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: a static dependency-graph architecture test proving compliance with a no-direct-DB-access rule is VerificationEvidence; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.25 — Stage 6: Runtime ... Verification→Runtime. Did the actual deployed system become what the implementation intended?
rows.statement: Defines the Verification->Runtime stage, asking whether the deployed system matches implementation intent.

rows.anchor: 117.26 — Experiment 12 ... Build artifact says Nexus:v2. Runtime actually runs Nexus:v1. Expected: Implementation≠Runtime. Result: DRIFT. This is exactly the type of problem a KnowledgeOS should eventually be able to represent.
rows.statement: Experiment 12: a build-artifact-vs-runtime version mismatch (v2 vs v1) is Implementation≠Runtime, classified DRIFT.

rows.anchor: 117.27 — Runtime identity ... RuntimeInstance connected to ArtifactVersion. Potentially DeploymentID.
rows.statement: Defines runtime identity as RuntimeInstance connected to ArtifactVersion and potentially DeploymentID.

rows.anchor: 117.28 — Experiment 13 ... Runtime reports artifact=nexus-pro:2.1, deployment=D-42. Expected: strong runtime identity evidence. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: a runtime report including artifact version and deployment ID is strong runtime identity evidence; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.29 — Stage 7: Observation ... Runtime state produces Observation. Nexus reachable, Repository count=43, Blob stores=40, Data size=256 GB. These are observations, not conclusions.
rows.statement: States raw runtime observations (reachability, counts, sizes) are observations, not conclusions.

rows.anchor: 117.30 — Experiment 14 ... Monitoring says Nexus container is healthy. Expected: Observation. It is not automatically ArchitectureConformant. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: a 'healthy' monitoring status is an Observation, not automatically ArchitectureConformant; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.31 — Observation → Evidence ... Observation: ContainerRunning=True supports Claim: DeploymentIsOperational. Observation-supports->Claim.
rows.statement: Defines Observation-supports->Claim, illustrated by ContainerRunning=True supporting DeploymentIsOperational.

rows.anchor: 117.32 — Experiment 15 ... Health check passes. Architecture Board decision required Nexus must run with rootless Podman. Runtime evidence confirms rootless operation. Expected: Observation→Evidence→Claim. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: runtime evidence confirming a required rootless-Podman condition demonstrates Observation->Evidence->Claim; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.33 — Stage 8: Updated knowledge ... Evidence→Knowledge. The result of the change should become part of the organization's current knowledge. This is more than a deployment log.
rows.statement: Defines Evidence->Knowledge: the result of a change should become part of current organizational knowledge, more than a deployment log.

rows.anchor: 117.34 — Experiment 16 ... Deployment completes. KnowledgeOS does not update the architecture state. Expected: RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState. Result: Knowledge synchronization gap
rows.statement: Experiment 16: a completed deployment with no corresponding architecture-state update leaves RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState, a knowledge synchronization gap.

rows.anchor: 117.35 — Closed-loop condition ... Intent→Decision→Authority→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Evidence→Knowledge. A genuine KnowledgeOS should eventually be able to reconstruct this path.
rows.statement: Restates the complete forward chain as the closed-loop condition a genuine KnowledgeOS should eventually reconstruct.

rows.anchor: 117.36 — The traceability matrix ... Intent/Decision/Authority/Implementation/Verification/Deployment/Runtime/Observation/Evidence/Knowledge, each with a Question and Evidence column. This becomes the canonical Engineering Traceability Record.
rows.statement: Presents the canonical ten-row Engineering Traceability Record template (stage x question x evidence).

rows.anchor: 117.37 — Four possible outcomes ... Outcome A Complete: EndToEndTraceability. Outcome B Technically complete: TechnicalTraceability. Outcome C Governance complete: GovernanceTraceability. Outcome D Fragmented: TraceabilityFragmentation.
rows.statement: Defines four possible traceability outcomes: Complete, Technically complete, Governance complete, Fragmented.

rows.anchor: 117.38 — Why this matters for KnowledgeOS ... KnowledgeOS should not merely answer 'Where is the architecture document?' It should answer 'Why does the current architecture exist, who authorized it, what implementation realizes it, and what evidence demonstrates that the deployed system still confor
rows.statement: Reframes KnowledgeOS's value proposition from document lookup to a full why/who/what/evidence-of-conformance capability.

rows.anchor: 117.39 — Agent use case ... An agent should be able to retrieve CurrentDecision, Authority, RelevantArchitecture, ImplementationConstraints, ExistingEvidence, KnownFindings. Then it can reason within an authoritative context.
rows.statement: States an agent handling a change request should retrieve six categories of authoritative context before reasoning.

rows.anchor: 117.40 — Experiment 17 ... Agent retrieves only Nexus migration documentation. Expected: useful contextual information, but not enough to establish CurrentAuthority. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: documentation-only retrieval is useful context but insufficient to establish CurrentAuthority; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.41 — Agent recommendation ... Agent can then produce Recommendation based on AuthoritativeKnowledge. But the recommendation remains AgentInference.
rows.statement: States agent recommendations remain AgentInference even when based on authoritative knowledge.

rows.anchor: 117.42 — Experiment 18 ... Agent recommends 'Use parallel deployment.' Expected: Recommendation. If the Architecture Board approves: Recommendation→Decision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: an agent recommendation becomes Decision only upon Architecture Board approval (Recommendation->Decision); result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.43 — Agent action ... Decision→DelegatedAuthority→AgentAction. This creates the bridge between governance and AI engineering.
rows.statement: Defines Decision->DelegatedAuthority->AgentAction as the bridge between governance and AI engineering.

rows.anchor: 117.44 — Experiment 19 ... Codex creates a pull request implementing an approved decision. Expected trace: Decision→CodexAction→PullRequest→Commit. Result: PASS provided the references are preserved.
rows.statement: Experiment 19: a Codex-implemented decision traces as Decision->CodexAction->PullRequest->Commit, conditional on preserved references; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.45 — Verification by agent ... The agent can then run Verification. But it must not simply report 'Looks good.' Instead Tool→DeterministicResult→Evidence.
rows.statement: Requires agent-run verification to follow Tool->DeterministicResult->Evidence, not a prose summary.

rows.anchor: 117.46 — Experiment 20 ... Codex runs architecture tests. All pass. Expected: VerificationEvidence. The agent's prose summary is secondary. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: agent-run passing architecture tests are VerificationEvidence, with the agent's prose summary secondary; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.47 — The agent assurance chain ... Authoritative Knowledge→Agent Context→Reasoning→Recommendation→Authorized Action→Deterministic Verification→Evidence→KnowledgeOS Update. This is the architecture we have been progressively reconstructing.
rows.statement: Presents the ideal agent assurance chain from Authoritative Knowledge through Agent Context/Reasoning/Recommendation/Authorized Action/Deterministic Verification/Evidence to KnowledgeOS Update.

rows.anchor: 117.48 — Failure experiment ... Agent reads stale memory, proposes a change, implements it, tests it, never checks current architecture authority. The technical result might be correct. But GovernanceTrace=Broken.
rows.statement: Presents a failure experiment: an agent acting on stale memory without checking current authority produces GovernanceTrace=Broken even if technically correct.

rows.anchor: 117.49 — Experiment 21 ... Agent's implementation passes all tests but violates an Architecture Board decision. Expected: TechnicalVerification=PASS but GovernanceConformance=FAIL. Result: PASS. Technical correctness does not imply organizational correctness.
rows.statement: Experiment 21: a test-passing but board-decision-violating implementation is TechnicalVerification=PASS/GovernanceConformance=FAIL, crystallizing the principle that technical correctness does not imply organizational correctness.

rows.anchor: 117.50 — Two-dimensional assurance ... TechnicalConformance and GovernanceConformance. Overall: Conformance=Technical∩Governance.
rows.statement: Defines two-dimensional assurance Conformance=Technical∩Governance.

rows.anchor: 117.51 — Experiment 22 ... Implementation is technically valid but not authorized. Expected: Technical=PASS, Governance=FAIL. Overall: FAIL. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: a technically-valid-but-unauthorized implementation yields overall FAIL under Conformance=Technical∩Governance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.52 — Conversely ... A decision may be fully authorized but technically incorrectly implemented. Then Governance=PASS, Technical=FAIL. Again Overall=FAIL.
rows.statement: Presents the converse case: a fully-authorized but technically-incorrect implementation also yields overall FAIL.

rows.anchor: 117.53 — KnowledgeOS assurance model ... Assurance=Evidence+Verification+Authority+Traceability rather than Assurance=TestResult.
rows.statement: Defines the KnowledgeOS assurance model Assurance=Evidence+Verification+Authority+Traceability, explicitly rejecting Assurance=TestResult.

rows.anchor: 117.54 — Traceability completeness ... T=verified links/required links. For important architecture decisions, a single missing critical edge can invalidate the trace. Therefore CriticalPath must be assessed separately.
rows.statement: Defines traceability completeness T=verified-links/required-links, requiring CriticalPath to be assessed separately since one missing edge can invalidate the trace.

rows.anchor: 117.55 — Critical path ... Authority→Decision→Action→Verification→Evidence is the minimal governance-assurance path.
rows.statement: Defines the critical path Authority->Decision->Action->Verification->Evidence as the minimal governance-assurance path.

rows.anchor: 117.56 — Experiment 23 ... All implementation artifacts exist. But no authority can be established. Expected: CriticalPath=Broken. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: complete implementation artifacts with no establishable authority yield CriticalPath=Broken; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.57 — Temporal reconstruction ... t_intent, t_decision, t_implementation, t_verification, t_deployment, t_observation. Then verify temporal consistency.
rows.statement: Defines temporal reconstruction across six timestamped stages, requiring consistency verification.

rows.anchor: 117.58 — Experiment 24 ... Verification timestamp t_v occurs before implementation t_i. Expected: potential invalid evidence or clock/data problem. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: a verification timestamp preceding its implementation timestamp is a potential invalid-evidence or clock/data problem; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.59 — Version reconstruction ... DecisionVersion must be connected to ImplementationVersion. Decision D42→Commit c81→Artifact v2.4.
rows.statement: Defines version reconstruction DecisionVersion->ImplementationVersion, illustrated by Decision D42->Commit c81->Artifact v2.4.

rows.anchor: 117.60 — Experiment 25 ... Commit implements an older superseded decision. Expected: potential governance mismatch. Result: OBS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: a commit implementing an already-superseded decision is a potential governance mismatch, classified OBS.

rows.anchor: 117.61 — Knowledge update ... KnowledgeOS should ideally record DecisionStatus and ImplementationStatus. The exact representation is implementation-specific.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS should ideally record DecisionStatus and ImplementationStatus alongside verification/runtime/knowledge status.

rows.anchor: 117.62 — Experiment 26 ... Decision remains Approved with no indication whether implementation occurred. Expected: governance state and engineering state are disconnected. Result: OBS
rows.statement: Experiment 26: a decision remaining 'Approved' with no implementation-status indication leaves governance and engineering state disconnected, classified OBS.

rows.anchor: 117.63 — The state reconciliation problem ... DeclaredState, ImplementationState, DeploymentState, RuntimeState, KnowledgeState. KnowledgeOS's role is potentially to reconcile these.
rows.statement: Defines five potentially divergent state realities, proposing KnowledgeOS's role as reconciling them.

rows.anchor: 117.64 — The reconciliation model ... Declared→Implemented→Deployed→Observed→Verified→Authoritative Knowledge. Every transition should have evidence.
rows.statement: Defines the reconciliation chain Declared->Implemented->Deployed->Observed->Verified->Authoritative Knowledge, every transition requiring evidence.

rows.anchor: 117.65 — Experiment 27 ... Declared, implementation, deployment, runtime all use PostgreSQL. Expected: strong conformance chain. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: PostgreSQL used consistently across declared/implementation/deployment/runtime is a strong conformance chain; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.66 — Experiment 28 ... Declared and implementation use PostgreSQL. Runtime uses MySQL. Expected: ArchitectureDrift. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: PostgreSQL declared/implemented but MySQL at runtime is ArchitectureDrift; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.67 — Finding generation ... When the graph detects Expected≠Observed, we can generate Finding. But Detection≠Finding until the system interprets the discrepancy according to a rule.
rows.statement: Reiterates Detection≠Finding: a rule must interpret Expected≠Observed before a Finding is generated.

rows.anchor: 117.68 — Experiment 29 ... Runtime differs from architecture. System creates ArchitectureDriftFinding with rule, observed state, expected state, evidence. Expected: strong semantic finding. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: a fully-fielded ArchitectureDriftFinding (rule/observed/expected/evidence) is a strong semantic finding; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.69 — Finding lifecycle ... Open→Investigating→Remediating→Verified→Closed. This connects the loop back to governance.
rows.statement: Defines the finding lifecycle Open->Investigating->Remediating->Verified->Closed, connecting back to governance.

rows.anchor: 117.70 — Experiment 30 ... Finding is marked Closed. No verification evidence exists. Expected: potential lifecycle integrity violation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: a Closed finding with no verification evidence is a potential lifecycle integrity violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 117.71 — The complete KnowledgeOS loop ... INTENT→DECISION→AUTHORITY→ENGINEERING ACTION→IMPLEMENTATION→DETERMINISTIC VERIFICATION→RUNTIME→OBSERVATION→EVIDENCE→KNOWLEDGE UPDATE→future INTENT. The cycle is Intent→Decision→Action→Reality→Evidence→Knowledge.
rows.statement: Presents the complete target-architecture cycle diagram from Intent through Knowledge Update back to future Intent.

rows.anchor: 117.72 — The decisive distinction ... A repository or knowledge base primarily stores State. An operating system manages State+Transitions+Control+Feedback. KnowledgeOS=Knowledge+StateTransitions+Governance+Evidence+Feedback is a much stronger architectural definition than 'AI knowledge platform.'
rows.statement: States the decisive distinction: a repository stores State, an operating system manages State+Transitions+Control+Feedback, formalized as KnowledgeOS=Knowledge+StateTransitions+Governance+Evidence+Feedback.

rows.anchor: 117.73 — Step 117 verdict ... Can one real change be traversed from intent to authoritative post-change knowledge? If yes, KnowledgeOS demonstrates operating-system characteristics. If the chain breaks, the missing edge identifies an architectural gap. STEP 117 — TRACEABILITY EXPERIMENT: DEFINED. Th
rows.statement: Records the Step 117 verdict DEFINED (not PASS/FAIL), with the actual implementation verdict explicitly left evidence-dependent.

rows.anchor: Step 118 — Governance-to-Engineering Closure Test preview ... We now test the reverse direction. When reality changes unexpectedly, can KnowledgeOS propagate that observation back into governance and authoritative knowledge? Runtime→Observation→Finding→Governance→Decision→Remediation→Verification. T
rows.statement: Previews Step 118: testing the reverse direction Runtime->Observation->Finding->Governance->Decision->Remediation->Verification, moving from traceability to closed-loop engineering control.

Intent→Decision→Authority→Implementation→Verific

aliases: Uncertainty Propagation, Dependence, Correlation, Error Propagation and Epistemic Risk

sources.note: S0928's Step 33: formalizes typed uncertainty (measurement/sampling/parameter/model/prediction/epistemic/aleatory), dependence/covariance-aware propagation, provenance-as-dependence-structure, Bayesian/frequentist/interval/set-valued representations, model and causal-structural uncertainty, Monte Carlo limits, confidence inflation, assumption-sensitivity graphs, and epistemic risk as consequence-weighted uncertainty. Its own opening places it immediately after Step 32 (S0926), but it was processed after Step 34 (S0927) in this batch's file order, and its closing section previews Step 34 content already extracted.

rows.anchor: Confidence_total = Confidence_1 x Confidence_2 x Confidence_3 ... That is generally wrong
rows.statement: Rejects naive multiplication of stage confidences as generally wrong; the correct propagation depends on uncertainty semantics and dependence.

lineage_claims.quote: We now continue from Step 32.

rows.anchor: Measurement uncertainty, Sampling uncertainty, Parameter uncertainty, Model uncertainty, Prediction uncertainty, Epistemic uncertainty, Aleatory variability ... must not automatically be collapsed into one number
rows.statement: Distinguishes at least seven kinds of uncertainty that must not be collapsed into one number.

rows.anchor: Aleatory variability: Variation inherent in the phenomenon ... Epistemic uncertainty: Uncertainty caused by incomplete knowledge ... Randomness != LackOfKnowledge
rows.statement: Formalizes the aleatory-vs-epistemic distinction with a travel-time/traffic example, giving the principle Randomness != LackOfKnowledge.

rows.anchor: Y=X+epsilon ... E[epsilon]=0 and Var(epsilon)=sigma^2 ... those assumptions themselves require justification
rows.statement: Formalizes a basic measurement-error model and warns its moment assumptions require justification.

rows.anchor: Y=h(X,theta,epsilon) ... KnowledgeOS should preserve the measurement model where available
rows.statement: Generalizes to a measurement model KnowledgeOS should preserve, else downstream models may treat measured values as exact.

rows.anchor: Var(Y) approx J Sigma J^T ... Jacobian ... covariance matrix ... exposes why independent multiplication of confidence values is inadequate
rows.statement: Formalizes first-order error propagation via the Jacobian and covariance matrix.

rows.anchor: Cov(X_i,X_j) != 0 ... Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y) ... Dependence matters
rows.statement: Formalizes covariance's role in propagation, giving the principle that dependence matters.

rows.anchor: E_1 and E_2 both come from the same underlying report. Treating them as independent could artificially increase certainty. This is a major risk in AI systems
rows.statement: States the evidence-duplication problem as a major risk in AI systems.

rows.anchor: E_1=f(S), E_2=g(S) ... E_1 not-perp E_2 ... combining them as independent evidence is invalid
rows.statement: Formalizes correlated evidence sharing a common source and invalidates treating it as independent.

rows.anchor: Provenance -> DependenceStructure -> CorrectUncertaintyPropagation ... This is a major result
rows.statement: States provenance's mathematical role: it enables estimating dependency and hence correct uncertainty propagation, called a major result.

rows.anchor: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) ... prior P(H) and likelihood P(E|H) must have explicit provenance and assumptions
rows.statement: Restates Bayesian updating and requires explicit provenance/assumptions for prior and likelihood.

rows.anchor: Not every knowledge problem has a meaningful prior ... BayesianUpdate must be a typed operation requiring a valid probabilistic model. It should not be the universal inference engine
rows.statement: Constrains Bayesian updating to be a typed operation requiring a valid model, not a universal inference engine.

rows.anchor: confidence intervals; sampling distributions; hypothesis tests; bootstrap distributions; asymptotic approximations ... theta-hat +- z SE(theta-hat) ... KnowledgeOS should preserve the framework
rows.statement: Lists frequentist uncertainty representations and requires preserving the inferential framework used.

rows.anchor: A standard confidence interval [L,U] should not automatically be interpreted as P(L<=theta<=U)=0.95. That interpretation is generally Bayesian, not classical frequentist
rows.statement: Warns against the common misinterpretation of a frequentist confidence interval as a Bayesian probability statement.

rows.anchor: X in [L,U] ... Latency in [100ms,150ms] ... No probability distribution is required
rows.statement: Defines interval uncertainty requiring no probability distribution, with a latency example.

rows.anchor: X in S where S is a feasible set ... useful when evidence constrains the possibilities without assigning probabilities
rows.statement: Generalizes interval uncertainty to set-valued uncertainty over a feasible set.

rows.anchor: X in [0,100] but have no justified distribution. The system should not invent X~Uniform(0,100) ... Bounded != Probabilistically Specified
rows.statement: Forbids inventing a uniform distribution over a bounded but unjustified range, giving the principle Bounded != Probabilistically Specified.

rows.anchor: theta in Theta_I ... PartiallyIdentified. This is stronger than simply saying uncertain
rows.statement: Introduces partial identification as a distinct, stronger-than-generic-uncertainty statistical concept.

rows.anchor: 10<=X<=20 and Y=2X ... 20<=Y<=40 ... propagated a set-valued constraint without inventing a probability distribution
rows.statement: Worked example of set-valued constraint propagation without inventing a distribution.

rows.anchor: X_1,X_2 -> Y -> Z ... KnowledgeOS should preserve DependencyGraph. Then uncertainty can be propagated through the graph
rows.statement: Defines a dependency graph structure for propagating uncertainty through a network.

rows.anchor: Sigma = [[sigma_1^2, sigma_12],[sigma_12, sigma_2^2]] ... off-diagonal terms matter. Ignoring them can substantially underestimate or overestimate uncertainty
rows.statement: Formalizes the correlation/covariance matrix and warns ignoring off-diagonal terms mis-estimates uncertainty.

rows.anchor: X_1=X_1*+epsilon_c+epsilon_1, X_2=X_2*+epsilon_c+epsilon_2 ... Cov(X_1,X_2)>0 ... KnowledgeOS needs provenance capable of identifying this common source
rows.statement: Formalizes common-source (shared calibration error) uncertainty and requires provenance able to identify it.

rows.anchor: M_1 and M_2 are both plausible models ... uncertainty exists not merely in parameters theta but in M. P(Y|X) may depend on model selection
rows.statement: Distinguishes model uncertainty from parameter uncertainty.

rows.anchor: P(Y|X) = sum_m P(Y|X,M_m)P(M_m|D) ... requires a probabilistic model over models. We should not automatically average incompatible models
rows.statement: Formalizes model averaging and constrains it to require a justified model-over-models, forbidding automatic averaging of incompatible models.

rows.anchor: X -> Y? versus X not-> Y ... This is structural/model uncertainty. It is distinct from uncertainty in theta
rows.statement: Distinguishes structural/relational uncertainty from parameter uncertainty.

rows.anchor: X<->Y does not establish X->Y. KnowledgeOS must distinguish Association from Causation. This prevents another major AI reasoning error
rows.statement: Requires distinguishing association from causation as prevention of a major AI reasoning error.

rows.anchor: X->Y or Y->X or Z->X,Z->Y. Observational evidence may not distinguish them. Therefore CausalIdentifiability must be explicitly represented
rows.statement: Requires explicit representation of causal (graph) identifiability given observationally indistinguishable causal structures.

rows.anchor: Y=2X+3, X in [1,2] => Y in [5,7] ... deterministic interval propagation. No probability is necessary
rows.statement: Worked example of deterministic interval propagation through a linear function.

rows.anchor: Y=X^2, X in [-2,3] => Y in [0,9]. Naive endpoint transformation [-2^2,3^2]=[4,9] would be wrong
rows.statement: Worked counterexample showing naive endpoint-based interval propagation through a nonlinear function is wrong.

rows.anchor: X~P_X and Y=f(X) ... sample X^(1),...,X^(N) ... compute Y^(i)=f(X^(i)) ... estimate P_Y. This is computationally feasible
rows.statement: Defines Monte Carlo propagation for sufficiently specified probabilistic models.

rows.anchor: If P_X is unjustified, Monte Carlo simply produces precise-looking results from an unjustified distribution ... Computational precision != Epistemic precision
rows.statement: States Monte Carlo cannot manufacture missing information, giving the principle Computational precision != Epistemic precision.

rows.anchor: Evidence->0.8 then Inference->0.9 then Decision->0.95 ... Confidence Inflation
rows.statement: Names the 'Confidence Inflation' failure mode where a reasoning chain manufactures unwarranted certainty.

rows.anchor: Any transformation that increases epistemic certainty must provide a mathematical reason ... LLMReasoning alone does not justify 0.8->0.95 ... CertaintyIncrease requires EvidenceOrValidInference
rows.statement: States the anti-inflation rule: certainty increase requires evidence or valid inference, not LLM reasoning alone.

rows.anchor: E->A->M->P->D ... each stage should declare its uncertainty semantics ... measurement uncertainty / interval uncertainty / parameter uncertainty / predictive distribution / expected-loss distribution
rows.statement: Requires each stage of the epistemic reasoning chain to declare explicit, distinct uncertainty semantics rather than an undifferentiated confidence number.

rows.anchor: UncertaintyType should be part of the epistemic type system. U_prob, U_interval, U_set, U_qualitative, U_unknown
rows.statement: Defines UncertaintyType as part of the epistemic type system with five example kinds.

rows.anchor: X in [0,10]. It is invalid to silently convert this to X~Uniform(0,10). Interval not-> Probability without an explicit modeling assumption
rows.statement: Forbids silent interval-to-probability conversion without an explicit modeling assumption.

rows.anchor: U_interval -> U_prob must require DistributionAssumption. That assumption becomes provenance
rows.statement: Frames the interval-to-probability conversion as an instance of epistemic type safety, requiring an assumption tracked as provenance.

rows.anchor: Assumption as a first-class object ... A_1: X~Uniform(0,10) ... DerivedProbability depends on A_1. If A_1 is challenged, downstream conclusions are affected
rows.statement: Defines Assumption as a first-class object whose invalidation affects downstream conclusions.

rows.anchor: G=(V,E) extended with Assumption nodes ... Assumption -> Model -> Prediction -> Decision. Extremely important for impact analysis
rows.statement: Extends the dependency graph with assumption nodes for impact analysis.

rows.anchor: D=f(A_1,A_2). If small changes in A_1 dramatically alter D, then Sensitivity(D,A_1) is high ... a mathematical basis for prioritizing validation
rows.statement: Defines sensitivity to assumptions as a mathematical basis for prioritizing validation.

rows.anchor: Sensitivity_i = |partial D / partial A_i| ... S_i can be defined using finite perturbations
rows.statement: Formalizes local sensitivity via partial derivatives or finite perturbations.

rows.anchor: variance decomposition ... Var(Y) = sum_i Contribution_i + Interactions ... identifies which uncertainties dominate the output
rows.statement: Extends to global sensitivity via variance decomposition for nonlinear systems.

rows.anchor: Risk(D) = E[Loss(D,Y)] ... EpistemicRisk includes uncertainty about the model/knowledge used to calculate the risk
rows.statement: Defines epistemic risk as risk that itself includes uncertainty about the model used to compute it.

rows.anchor: Uncertainty asks What do we not know? Risk asks What is the consequence of uncertain outcomes? Risk=f(Uncertainty,Consequences)
rows.statement: Distinguishes risk from uncertainty as consequence-weighted uncertainty.

rows.anchor: P(Failure)=0.01. For a harmless experiment Risk may be negligible. For a catastrophic system Risk may be unacceptable. uncertainty alone does not determine action
rows.statement: Worked example showing identical failure probability yields different risk depending on consequence severity.

rows.anchor: EL(a)=E[L(a,Y)] ... a* = argmin_a EL(a)
rows.statement: Formalizes standard decision-theoretic expected loss and the optimal decision.

rows.anchor: EL(a|M_1) != EL(a|M_2) ... model uncertainty affects the decision
rows.statement: States model uncertainty propagates into decision-relevant expected-loss differences.

rows.anchor: a* = argmin_a sup_{P in mathcal P} E_P[L(a,Y)] ... a robust decision approach ... rather than forcing one probability distribution
rows.statement: Formalizes a minimax robust-decision alternative for insufficiently justified probability models.

rows.anchor: We do not need PerfectKnowledge before every action. We need SufficientKnowledge for the decision's risk and constraints. DecisionQuality depends on required epistemic resolution
rows.statement: States decision quality depends on required, not perfect, epistemic resolution.

rows.anchor: For a trivial decision LowRisk a rough estimate may be enough. For CriticalAction ... RequiredEvidence = f(DecisionCriticality)
rows.statement: Formalizes required evidence as a function of decision criticality.

rows.anchor: The domain determines DecisionCriticality. Statistics determines Uncertainty. Governance determines RequiredAssurance. KnowledgeOS orchestrates these but should not own their domain semantics
rows.statement: Distinguishes the domain-owned, statistics-owned, and governance-owned roles that KnowledgeOS orchestrates without owning.

rows.anchor: UncertaintyBudget ... U(D)<=U_max ... requires MoreEvidence or HumanReview
rows.statement: Introduces an uncertainty budget for critical decisions with an escalation response when exceeded.

rows.anchor: We should not define a universal U_max=0.1 ... U_max(Context,Decision)
rows.statement: Rejects a universal uncertainty-budget threshold in favor of a context/decision-specific one.

rows.anchor: High-quality evidence does not necessarily eliminate uncertainty ... EvidenceQuality != ZeroUncertainty
rows.statement: Distinguishes evidence quality from zero uncertainty given irreducible aleatory variance.

rows.anchor: P(Y=1|X)=0.7. Even with perfect knowledge of the model, the outcome remains stochastic. Uncertainty can be irreducible
rows.statement: Worked example establishing that uncertainty can be irreducible even given a perfectly known model.

rows.anchor: Additional evidence may reduce Var(theta|E) or shrink Theta_I. InformationAcquisition -> UncertaintyReduction. This is the bridge toward the later Value-of-Information problem
rows.statement: States epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by evidence, explicitly bridging to the Value-of-Information problem (Step 34).

lineage_claims.quote: This is the bridge toward the later Value-of-Information problem.

rows.anchor: New evidence reveals that our previous model was oversimplified. Uncertainty_new > Uncertainty_old. This may represent better calibrated knowledge. LowerReportedUncertainty is not always evidence of better knowledge
rows.statement: States more evidence can increase reported uncertainty while representing an epistemic improvement, contradicting the assumption that lower uncertainty is always better.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS should prefer AccurateUncertainty over ArtificialCertainty. A newly discovered uncertainty is often an epistemic improvement
rows.statement: States the epistemic-honesty principle preferring accurate over artificial certainty.

rows.anchor: Experiments A-E: shared-source evidence naively independent->DependenceDetected/IndependenceUnknown PASS; interval->uniform conversion without assumption->InvalidConversion PASS; unknown distribution fed to Monte Carlo->NoSimulation PASS; correlated inputs treated independent->DependenceWarning PASS
rows.statement: Runs falsification tests A-E (all PASS): evidence-duplication is flagged rather than silently treated as independent; illegal interval-to-uniform conversion is rejected; Monte Carlo on an unjustified distribution is refused; correlated-but-treated-independent inputs raise a dependence warning; and an LLM-driven unsupported confidence jump is rejected.

experiment.hypothesis: KnowledgeOS's uncertainty-typing and dependence-tracking rules correctly reject naive/unjustified uncertainty manipulations.
experiment.setup: Five scenarios: shared-source duplicate evidence, illegal interval-to-distribution conversion, unjustified Monte Carlo input, correlated-but-untracked inputs, and unsupported LLM confidence inflation.
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply dependence-detection, type-safety, and anti-inflation rules to each scenario
experiment.result: all five scenarios produce the expected rejection/flag
experiment.interpretation: confirms the type-safety and dependence rules catch the intended failure modes
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All five tests PASS.

rows.anchor: Experiments F-J: new evidence reveals unknown uncertainty source->ReportedUncertainty may increase, not automatically worse PASS; low-probability catastrophic-loss decision->risk analysis flags unacceptable loss PASS; two models produce materially different decisions->ModelUncertainty->DecisionSensi
rows.statement: Runs falsification tests F-J (all PASS): a newly revealed uncertainty source is not automatically classified as worse knowledge; a low-probability catastrophic decision is correctly flagged as high risk; model disagreement is correctly linked to decision sensitivity; assumption invalidation correctly triggers closure-based impact identification; and a deterministic transformation yields exactly zero output uncertainty only when both transformation and inputs are exact.

experiment.hypothesis: The risk, model-uncertainty, assumption-closure, and deterministic-propagation rules behave correctly under adversarial/edge scenarios.
experiment.setup: Five scenarios: newly-revealed uncertainty, low-probability/high-consequence risk, conflicting models, invalidated assumption, and exact deterministic propagation.
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the risk/closure/propagation rules to each scenario
experiment.result: all five scenarios produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: confirms epistemic honesty, risk-consequence weighting, and closure-based impact analysis work as intended
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed
experiment.conclusion: All five tests PASS.

rows.anchor: STEP 33 — PASS. But this step produced several important architectural rules
rows.statement: Step 33 self-verdict: PASS.

rows.anchor: Principle 1: Uncertainty is typed ... Principle 2: Dependence is first-class ... Principle 3: Precision is not knowledge ... Principle 4: Certainty cannot be manufactured ... Principle 5: Unknown distributions remain unknown
rows.statement: States the first five of ten boxed architectural principles from Step 33: uncertainty must be explicitly typed; evidence independence must never be assumed from separate records alone; computational precision does not equal epistemic precision; certainty increase requires evidence/valid inference/explicit assumption; and unknown distributions must never be treated as uniform.

rows.anchor: Principle 6: Model uncertainty is real uncertainty ... Principle 7: Risk is consequence-weighted uncertainty ... Principle 8: Evidence can reduce or reveal uncertainty ... Principle 9: Uncertainty must propagate through dependencies ... Principle 10: Critical decisions require epistemic thresholds
rows.statement: States the remaining five of ten boxed architectural principles: parameter uncertainty != model uncertainty, both must be represented; risk = E[L(a,Y)], not a naive product shorthand; knowledge improvement does not always mean lower uncertainty; uncertainty propagation through dependencies has no universal multiplication rule; and critical decisions exceeding an uncertainty threshold require no automatic execution (acquire evidence, validate, human review, or choose a robust action).

rows.anchor: REALITY->OBSERVATION->EVIDENCE (Provenance/Dependence)->EPISTEMIC CLAIM (Time/Context/Uncertainty)->MODEL (Params/Structure/Assumptions)->PREDICTION (Uncertainty)->DECISION (Utility/Risk)->ASSURANCE GATE (Constraints/Preconditions/Epistemic threshold)->ACTION->OUTCOME->VALIDATION->KNOWLEDGE REVISION
rows.statement: Presents an updated end-to-end architecture diagram incorporating provenance/dependence, epistemic-claim typing, model assumptions, and an assurance gate with epistemic threshold.

rows.anchor: U_D = U_measurement + U_sampling + U_model + U_state ... only schematic; these components cannot always simply be added
rows.statement: Presents a schematic four-component decomposition of decision uncertainty, explicitly noting components are not always simply additive.

rows.anchor: Did we measure the world accurately? Did we observe enough? Did we choose the correct model? Do we correctly understand the current state/context? These are different failure modes
rows.statement: Poses four uncertainty-diagnosis questions corresponding to four distinct failure modes.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS must preserve the semantics, source, dependencies and type of uncertainty whenever knowledge is transformed ... UncertaintySemantics(Y) = Transform(UncertaintySemantics(X), Assumptions(f), Model(f)) ... It may change. But it must not change silently
rows.statement: Formulates a strong architectural contract requiring uncertainty semantics to transform explicitly and never silently under any knowledge transformation.

rows.anchor: Step 29: Consistency; Step 30: External Validation; Step 31: Formalization; Step 32: Epistemic Algebra; Step 33: Uncertainty Propagation ... a coherent progression rather than a collection of disconnected ideas
rows.statement: Restates the Step 29-33 progression as a coherent mathematical development.

sources.note: STEP-TRACE batch B5: a full 66-file trace of 2026-08-28 morning (steps 25H-25Z and 26-66), the day the corpus produced its most extensive formal-verification apparatus (20 global invariants I1-I20 at step 48, an 8-primitive candidate kernel at step 49, a 20-counterexample audit and an information-theoretic impossibility/identifiability proof at step 31, a 50-attack consistency audit at step 50, and an 'executable reference model' at steps 51/55/56) while a corpus-wide grep for any executable code fence across all 66 files returns zero hits. Documents the batch's dominant defect, PASS-inflation (~880 PASS tokens, 0 executions, 0 FAILs), alongside the corpus's own strongest anti-inflation language (Specification!=Proof, the refusal to numericize P(ModelCorrect|Tests), the specified-vs-executed guard). Registers four worsened known contradictions (C-1 tuple wars now seven incompatible state tuples, C-2 status drift, C-3 monotonicity scoping, C-4 PASS-inflation) and five new ones (N-1 frozen-invariant-set violated by an unrenumbered 21st invariant, N-2 lattice-status reversal, N-3 the specified-vs-executed boundary itself violated within one file, N-4 an unmet four-artifact mandate, N-5 five topics each independently re-derived three times with no reconciliation).

rows.anchor: 25N (094210) -- Evidence Aggregation Algebra. FIRST PRINCIPLE (section25N.1): "evidence is not a scalar". SIX SEPARATE CONCEPTS: Support, Reliability, Authority, Probability, Confidence, Independence. ... IMPOSSIBILITY-STYLE RESULT ... Evidence has no intrinsic universal weight
rows.statement: Step 25H (092308) formalizes a governed Sarathi decision operator S(K,G,D,M,C) -> DecisionResult in {Decision, HumanDecisionRequired, InsufficientKnowledge, GovernanceBlocked, ModelUnderspecified}, with probability treated as optional (decisions may rest on constraints/dominance alone) and three decision modes (deterministic/model-based/human-escalation). Step 25N (094210) states as a first principle that evidence is not a scalar, decomposing it into six separate concepts (Support, Reliability, Authority, Probability, Confidence, Independence), gives the likelihood-ratio combination law LR(E1..En)=product of LR(Ei) under conditional independence while flagging independence as an assumption never to be auto-applied, distinguishes a Statistical aggregation regime from a Qualitative one that must never be silently mixed, and derives by counter-scenario (high-authority/low-reliability versus low-authority/high-reliability evidence) an impossibility-style result that evidence aggregation is domain/model dependent, boxed as 'Evidence has no intrinsic universal weight' with effect instead modeled as a relation Effect(E,A|C,M).

assumptions.statement: conditional independence used in likelihood-ratio combination is an assumption that must never be auto-applied
assumptions.anchor: independence is an assumption -- must never be auto-applied

rows.anchor: 25K (093925) -- Knowledge State Algebra and Closure. K = 11 fields ... universal monotonicity FAIL, universal commutativity FAIL, universal associativity FAIL; section25K.49 reframes the three FAILs as "not failures".
rows.statement: Step 25K defines an 11-field knowledge state K=(Assertions,Evidence,Provenance,Relations,Assessments,Validity,TemporalState,Conflicts,Versions,Contracts,Policies) with the event log kept conceptually separate, states six invariants (determinism, idempotence, provenance preservation, contradiction preservation, no-hallucinated-resolution, and monotonicity-only-carefully), and an eight-test closure result table that finds universal monotonicity, universal commutativity, and universal associativity all FAIL, immediately reframed as 'not failures' in the next section -- a reframing the trace later flags (as contradiction C-3) because these three negative results are never carried forward into Step 31's audit, Step 48's invariant set, or Step 51's invariant tests, quietly dropping out of the record while downstream summaries report uniform PASS.

lineage_claims.quote: The three FAILs from 25K.48 are never carried into Step 31's audit, Step 48's invariant set, or Step 51's INV tests

rows.anchor: Step 26 (101406) ... KEY DERIVATION (section26.5): epistemic Zero arises from observational equivalence -- Zero is given an information-theoretic ground ... section26.7 "identifiability is more important than confidence".
rows.statement: Step 26 grounds epistemic Zero in observational equivalence (two world states that produce the same observation are indistinguishable in principle, not merely unmeasured), argues identifiability matters more than confidence, defines observational equivalence, identifiability, model validity region, domain of applicability, an abstraction function with leakage, an observability matrix, and an instrumentation gap; distinguishes safe sensing from world-changing action; and derives six boxed inequalities (Model!=Reality, Observation!=State, Computability!=Justifiability, Confidence!=Identifiability, Correlation!=Causation, and that Unknown does not mean the system should guess), giving the system a way to state 'I cannot know this from the currently available observations' as distinct from ordinary uncertainty.
missing: an algorithm for detecting observational equivalence in practice

rows.anchor: Step 27 (101458) ... DEF (verbatim, section27.13): uncertainty is a vector U(H)=(U_measurement,U_epistemic,U_aleatoric,U_model,U_semantic,U_identity,U_temporal,U_causal) -- 8 components. ... TUPLE (section27.71): KnowledgeState = (Assertions,Evidence,Uncertainty,TemporalState,SemanticState,Provenance,Models,Rules) -- 8 fields
rows.statement: Step 27 defines uncertainty as an 8-component vector U(H)=(measurement, epistemic, aleatoric, model, semantic, identity, temporal, causal), argues probability requires a reference class or model, treats Dempster-Shafer as bounded rather than adopted, and separately states an 8-field KnowledgeState tuple, a 6-field DecisionState, and a 5-field ActionState; replaces a naive 'Confidence: 87%' with a 12-field worked assertion record. States seven boxed non-equivalences including Unknown!=0.5 and EvidenceStrength!=Probability. The trace notes that step 31.24 later silently narrows this 8-component uncertainty vector to a 5-field descriptor under the same notation U(H), an unremarked change (a new contradiction instance).
missing: a propagation calculus over the 8-component uncertainty vector

lineage_claims.quote: Step 31 silently narrows Step 27's uncertainty vector to a 5-field descriptor and never notes the change.

rows.anchor: Step 29 (101614) ... section29.24 the architectural discipline: "do we need an SMT solver everywhere? No" ... section29.31 "constraint confidence is unnecessary" ... section29.67 (the honest gap): "an internally consistent knowledge base can still be completely wrong"
rows.statement: Step 29 formalizes satisfiability (SAT(K and C) -> SAT/UNSAT) and satisfiability-modulo-theories for constraints like Version bounds, states the architectural discipline that solvers should be used only where complexity justifies them (not universally), catalogues eight constraint classes (Structural, Temporal, Semantic, Cardinality, Authorization, Safety, Statistical, Causal), argues constraints are typed, not probabilistic ('constraint confidence is unnecessary'), introduces a consistency vector generalizing a single consistency score plus unit/dimensional-analysis consistency (judged genuinely novel in the corpus), and prefers a Generate->Verify->Accept pipeline over Generate->Trust. Ends with an honest, load-bearing admission (section 29.67) that an internally consistent knowledge base can still be completely wrong (InternallyConsistent and ExternallyIncorrect can co-occur), explicitly handed off to step 30.
missing: a solver-encoding of the actual knowledge state

rows.anchor: Step 30 (102009) ... seven drift species -- model, data, concept, label, semantic, governance, reality drift ... section30.46 "drift detection can itself fail" -> section30.47 raised to fundamental epistemic invariant ... False != Unvalidated
rows.statement: Step 30 builds a validation hierarchy with Brier score and log loss for calibration, distinguishes calibration from discrimination, catalogues seven distinct drift species (model, data, concept, label, semantic, governance, and reality drift), introduces freshness/epistemic-decay/time-to-obsolescence, validator independence, the principle that validation is itself evidence, that ground truth can be revised, a validation predicate requiring Inconclusive as an essential third outcome (False != Unvalidated), and elevates 'drift detection can itself fail' to a fundamental epistemic invariant; introduces validation debt and knowledge decay as technical debt, and explicitly declines to produce a single reality-alignment score. States five boxed non-equivalences (Consistency!=Correctness, Validation!=Truth, NotValidated!=Invalid, NoDetectedDrift!=NoDrift, single-PredictionError!=ModelFailure).
missing: outcome data needed to bootstrap empirical calibration

rows.anchor: Step 31 (102251) ... section31.19: if Omega(W1)=Omega(W2) while W1!=W2, then "No algorithm can recover information that the observation function destroys." ... This is not a limitation of AI. It is an information-theoretic limitation. Classification: PROVEN-style
rows.statement: Step 31 (76 sections, the largest single formal artifact in the batch) gives 45 one-line definitional sections (typed universe with Observations/Evidence/Assertions/Models/Constraints/Decisions/Actions/Validation/Conflicts as genuinely different types; a 7-field knowledge state K_t=(E_t,A_t,M_t,C_t,F_t,V_t,R_t); a partial transition delta:K x Event -> K; a provenance graph; EpistemicTypeSafety forbidding silent casts like Hypothesis->ValidatedAssertion), then states what the trace judges the strongest formal result in the whole batch: an information-theoretic impossibility result (section 31.19) -- if two distinct world states produce the same observation, no algorithm can recover the information the observation function destroyed, explicitly stated as not an AI limitation but an information-theoretic one -- immediately followed by a formal identifiability definition (31.20) and the derivation that a non-identifiable quantity must be reported as Underdetermined (31.21), both classified PROVEN-style (correct, if elementary, formal arguments) rather than merely asserted.

rows.anchor: The 20 counterexamples ... CE11 hidden circularity A->M->V->A ... PASS conceptually. Formal implementation remains to be specified. ... CE20 all constraints satisfied but K not approx W -> InternalConsistency=True and ExternalValidity=False/Unknown -- PASS, annotated "perhaps the most important test".
rows.statement: Step 31 runs 20 narrative counterexamples (CE1-CE20) against its own formal apparatus, covering conflicting versions, missing evidence yielding Underdetermined rather than a guess, model disagreement versus contradiction, hallucinated action denial, preserved history for defeated assertions, out-of-domain model applicability, hidden derivation circularity (the only counterexample with a qualified verdict, 'PASS conceptually, formal implementation remains to be specified'), statistical constraint violation, invalid inference from Unknown, provenance integrity, cross-context rule misapplication, semantic type violation, revalidation requirements, calibration failure, and CE20 (internal consistency co-occurring with external invalidity/unknownness, annotated as perhaps the most important test); all 20 pass, all classified CONCEPTUAL_ONLY since none was executed. A twelve-category audit (31.69) then finds most categories PASS or PASS-conceptually, but epistemic type safety only PROMISING, and formal uncertainty propagation, complete proof calculus, and computational complexity all left OPEN.

experiment.hypothesis: Whether 20 designed adversarial counterexamples reveal a flaw in the step-31 formal model.
experiment.setup: 20 narrative scenarios each targeting a specific formal claim.
experiment.inputs: The step-31 type system, transition function, and invariants.
experiment.method: Walk through each scenario by hand and determine the expected system response.
experiment.result: All 20 scenarios produce the expected, non-contradictory response.
experiment.interpretation: The model is structurally sound at least against the tested scenarios.
experiment.limitations: Purely narrative; no software was run; no coverage argument connects the 20 cases to the full state/invariant space.
experiment.conclusion: Internal contradiction detected: NONE SO FAR (self-reported), but three OPEN audit categories remain.

rows.anchor: Step 32 (102341) ... section32.79 new atomic object: EpistemicClaim = (Subject,Predicate,Value,Context,Time,Evidence,Provenance,EpistemicStatus,Uncertainty,Validation,Dependencies) -- 11 fields, and it displaces Fact. ... three failure states False / Unknown / Undefined
rows.statement: Step 32 constructs the core epistemic algebra K-fraktur=(K-calligraphic, preceq, compose, oplus, Revision, Validate, Infer, Conflict), sharpens the two-valued False/Unknown into three failure states False/Unknown/Undefined, distinguishes information ordering from truth ordering, states that evidence addition is monotonic under the information order while revision is non-monotonic, separates an accumulating evidence layer from a belief layer that may change interpretation, and introduces an 11-field EpistemicClaim=(Subject,Predicate,Value,Context,Time,Evidence,Provenance,EpistemicStatus,Uncertainty,Validation,Dependencies) that explicitly displaces the earlier concept of Fact as the atomic epistemic object.

rows.anchor: Step 34 (102459) ... boxed formula I*=argmax_I[EVSI(I)-Cost(I)] subject to constraints. Classification DERIVED (standard decision-analytic result, correctly stated). This is the sharpest operational formula in the batch.
rows.statement: Step 34 formalizes information acquisition using EVPI and EVSI, culminating in the boxed operational formula I* = argmax_I [EVSI(I) - Cost(I)] subject to constraints, selecting the next-best epistemic action; judged the sharpest operational (correctly-stated standard decision-analytic) formula in the batch and classified DERIVED rather than merely asserted.

rows.anchor: Step 36 (102624) ... Object level vs meta level ... A knowledge system must be evaluated not only by the correctness of its outputs, but by the calibration of its epistemic processes. ... Step 37 (102747) ... the neutral-source assumption must be removed
rows.statement: Step 36 introduces meta-epistemology as a distinct architectural layer, distinguishing calibration from accuracy and from confidence, and states the boxed meta-principle that a knowledge system must be evaluated not only by the correctness of its outputs but by the calibration of its own epistemic processes -- judged genuinely new relative to step 30's object-level calibration. Step 37 introduces the only adversary-with-incentives model in the batch, distinguishing random error, systematic bias, and strategic manipulation, and states that the neutral-source assumption must be removed, making EpistemicIntegrity first-class and extending the uncertainty taxonomy beyond aleatory sources; the largest file in the batch by size.

rows.anchor: Step 41 ... formally separating Knowledge from DecisionSufficiency. Step 42 ... moves from "knows enough" to "can formally determine whether a decision is admissible". Step 44 ... boxed: A decision changes the future state space. Step 47 ... self-generated evidence; confirmation loop; policy-induced distribution shift.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 25N (094210) -- Evidence Aggregation Algebra. FIRST PRINCIPLE (section25N.1): "evidence is not a scalar". SIX SEPARATE CONCEPTS: Support, Reliability, Authority, Probability, Confidence, Independence. ... IMPOSSIBILITY-STYLE RESULT ... Evidence has no intrinsic universal weight
rationale_evidence.statement: Step 25H (092308) formalizes a governed Sarathi decision operator S(K,G,D,M,C) -> DecisionResult in {Decision, HumanDecisionRequired, InsufficientKnowledge, GovernanceBlocked, ModelUnderspecified}, with probability treated as optional (decisions may rest on constraints/dominance alone) and three decision modes (deterministic/model-based/human-escalation). Step 25N (094210) states as a first principle that evidence is not a scalar, decomposing it into six separate concepts (Support, Reliability, Authority, Probability, Confidence, Independence), gives the likelihood-ratio combination law LR(E1..En)=product of LR(Ei) under conditional independence while flagging independence as an assumption never to be auto-applied, distinguishes a Statistical aggregation regime from a Qualitative one that must never be silently mixed, and derives by counter-scenario (high-authority/low-reliability versus low-authority/high-reliability evidence) an impossibility-style result that evidence aggregation is domain/model dependent, boxed as 'Evidence has no intrinsic universal weight' with effect instead modeled as a relation Effect(E,A|C,M).

rationale_evidence.statement: Step 26 grounds epistemic Zero in observational equivalence (two world states that produce the same observation are indistinguishable in principle, not merely unmeasured), argues identifiability matters more than confidence, defines observational equivalence, identifiability, model validity region, domain of applicability, an abstraction function with leakage, an observability matrix, and an instrumentation gap; distinguishes safe sensing from world-changing action; and derives six boxed inequalities (Model!=Reality, Observation!=State, Computability!=Justifiability, Confidence!=Identifiability, Correlation!=Causation, and that Unknown does not mean the system should guess), giving the system a way to state 'I cannot know this from the currently available observations' as distinct from ordinary uncertainty.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Step 29 (101614) ... section29.24 the architectural discipline: "do we need an SMT solver everywhere? No" ... section29.31 "constraint confidence is unnecessary" ... section29.67 (the honest gap): "an internally consistent knowledge base can still be completely wrong"
rationale_evidence.statement: Step 29 formalizes satisfiability (SAT(K and C) -> SAT/UNSAT) and satisfiability-modulo-theories for constraints like Version bounds, states the architectural discipline that solvers should be used only where complexity justifies them (not universally), catalogues eight constraint classes (Structural, Temporal, Semantic, Cardinality, Authorization, Safety, Statistical, Causal), argues constraints are typed, not probabilistic ('constraint confidence is unnecessary'), introduces a consistency vector generalizing a single consistency score plus unit/dimensional-analysis consistency (judged genuinely novel in the corpus), and prefers a Generate->Verify->Accept pipeline over Generate->Trust. Ends with an honest, load-bearing admission (section 29.67) that an internally consistent knowledge base can still be completely wrong (InternallyConsistent and ExternallyIncorrect can co-occur), explicitly handed off to step 30.

rationale_evidence.statement: Step 31 (76 sections, the largest single formal artifact in the batch) gives 45 one-line definitional sections (typed universe with Observations/Evidence/Assertions/Models/Constraints/Decisions/Actions/Validation/Conflicts as genuinely different types; a 7-field knowledge state K_t=(E_t,A_t,M_t,C_t,F_t,V_t,R_t); a partial transition delta:K x Event -> K; a provenance graph; EpistemicTypeSafety forbidding silent casts like Hypothesis->ValidatedAssertion), then states what the trace judges the strongest formal result in the whole batch: an information-theoretic impossibility result (section 31.19) -- if two distinct world states produce the same observation, no algorithm can recover the information the observation function destroyed, explicitly stated as not an AI limitation but an information-theoretic one -- immediately followed by a formal identifiability definition (31.20) and the derivation that a non-identifiable quantity must be reported as Underdetermined (31.21), both classified PROVEN-style (correct, if elementary, formal arguments) rather than merely asserted.

rationale_evidence.anchor: C-4 (PASS-INFLATION) -- the dominant defect of this batch. Evidence: ~880 PASS tokens, 0 executions, 0 FAILs across 60 steps. ... Mitigating and worth recording: this batch also contains the corpus's strongest anti-inflation language
rationale_evidence.statement: Names PASS-inflation the dominant defect of the entire batch: approximately 880 occurrences of the string PASS, zero executions, and zero FAILs across 60 substantive steps. Identifies four specific mechanisms: titular overclaim (a step titled 'Build and Execute' contains neither); terminology creep (a list of thirteen unproven capabilities labeled 'Proven/computable' in step 25N); qualified PASS silently aggregated as unqualified PASS (13 of step 50's 50 attacks pass only conditionally, yet the aggregate reads Counterexample=empty-set); and conditional PASS treated as a final verdict across six later steps. Notes as a mitigating, worth-recording fact that this same batch also contains the corpus's strongest anti-inflation language (Specification!=Proof, the refusal to numericize P(ModelCorrect|Tests), the step-55 specified-vs-executed guard, step-56's three-level ladder) -- concluding the authors were not unaware of the problem, but that awareness lived in prose while the indexed verdict tokens remained uniformly PASS regardless.

The verifier nonetheless identifies a specific short list of genuinely strong content recommended for the eventual survivor theory: step-058's authorization-validity-at-side-effect result, step-063's NotIdentified/Identifiability-not-Computability distinction, step-066's proved observational-indistinguishability claim (judged the only proved claim in the entire batch) and its clean five-way epistemic-limitation taxonomy, step-064's model-validity governance layer, step-061's typed non-scalar quality discipline, and step-060's restraint in refusing to declare a lattice structure -- though this restraint is itself undercut by the file's own un-derived boxed claim that the structure is nonetheless 'partially ordered.'

rationale_evidence.anchor: TV-F-033 -- Citation collapse: two cross-step citations in ~22,000 lines. ... Step-062 re-derives step-025R almost line for line ... VERIFIER OBSERVATION. rationale_evidence.statement: TV-F-033 finds that across the 11 files of the 056-066 band (approximately 22,000 lines), exactly two cross-step citations exist, while the band silently re-derives content from at least 15 earlier steps without citation, with specific sharp instances: step-062 re-derives step-025R's decision-theory apparatus almost line for line (renaming 'admissible' to 'feasible', re-presenting its VOI construction as EVSI) while naming none of 025R, 025H, 041, 042, 034, or 015; step-063 re-derives steps 025P and 043 wholesale (do-calculus, ATE, the backdoor formula, even a subgroup-heterogeneity result) while explicitly and falsely claiming 'we are not adding mathematical concepts randomly, each new layer emerged because the previous layer exposed a boundary' -- a claim the verifier judges false for this specific file, since the layer already existed at 014/025P/043; step-065 re-derives step-025U's central result (agreement != independent evidence) under a renamed symbol; and the evidence-independence result itself is independently re-derived four separate times within this one phase alone. States the load-bearing meta-conclusion: this citation collapse is not a documentation defect but the actual production mechanism generating the corpus's known formal regressions (TV-F-028) and namespace collisions (TV-F-022), since each re-derivation freely re-chooses symbols and re-selects formalization depth with no obligation to match what already exists.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The last row is decisive. There is no obvious primitive in K5 corresponding to: A=Action.
rationale_evidence.statement: A component-by-component comparison of K8=(E,S,T,O,P,R,Pi,A) against K5=(G,sigma,theta,lambda,pi) finds a strongest correspondence for Pi<->pi but no obvious K5 component corresponding to Action (A); therefore a direct surjective reduction K8->K5 already loses an explicit K8 dimension unless Action is shown to be externally derived, which has not been demonstrated.

rationale_evidence.anchor: K8 contains explicit ontological categories ... K5 contains ... These are not simply different names for the same eight/five components. Therefore: K_8 \not\equiv K_5 (current evidence)
rationale_evidence.statement: Rejects the direct-equivalence hypothesis K8 cong K5 on current evidence: K8's categories (Entity, State, Event, Observation, Proposition, Relation, Policy, Action) and K5's categories (Graph, EpistemicStatus, TemporalValidity, Lineage, Policy) are not simply renamings of each other; explicitly notes this does not mean the two are incompatible, only that direct equivalence fails.

rationale_evidence.anchor: For K5⊆K8, we would need to construct G=f(E,S,T,O,P,R,...) ... But these mappings are precisely the mappings that Step 242 told us must not be assumed. Therefore: K_5\subseteq K_8: UNPROVEN ... Thus: K_8\subseteq K_5: NOT ESTABLISHED
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests both conservative-extension directions between K5 and K8: K5⊆K8 would require unproven derivation functions (G=f(E,S,T,O,P,R,...), sigma=f_sigma(...), theta=f_theta(S,T), lambda=f_lambda(T,R,O), pi=f_pi(Pi,A)) that Step 242 forbade assuming; K8⊆K5 is even less supported since Action (A) has no explicit K5 counterpart at all. Both directions rated UNPROVEN/NOT ESTABLISHED.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Coverage(K_8)=HIGH but Closure(K_8)=UNPROVEN. ... Coverage(K_5)=PARTIAL at the present formal level.
rationale_evidence.statement: Scores each kernel candidate against requirement set R: K8 directly covers Entity,State,Event,Observation,Proposition,Relation,Policy,Action (Coverage=HIGH) but omits Uncertainty (Closure=UNPROVEN); K5 directly covers Relation, EpistemicStatus, TemporalValidity, Lineage, Policy (Coverage=PARTIAL) but leaves Identity, Evidence, Uncertainty, Action and Proposition semantics undefined.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Are K8 and K5 objects of the same type? If NO: What are their types and what is the formal mapping between their layers? If YES: Construct the mapping explicitly. Do not use semantic similarity as proof.
rationale_evidence.statement: Requires K8=(E,S,T,O,P,R,Pi,A) and K5=(G,sigma,theta,lambda,pi) each be reconstructed as typed objects over the formal universe (not reduced to each other), then requires an explicit typing verdict (same type with an explicit mapping, or different types with an explicit inter-layer mapping) -- reiterating that semantic name-similarity is never proof.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The question is now: lambda sufficient to make the state abstraction transformation-compatible? We do not know yet. ... K8 explicitly includes T and A alongside historical/provenance-related structures. That gives it greater expressive capacity. But greater expressive capacity does not imply minimal
rationale_evidence.statement: Applies the new congruence-based sufficiency criterion to both K5 and K8, concluding neither is validated: it remains unknown whether K5's lambda alone is sufficient for transformation-compatibility, and K8's greater expressive richness (including T and A) is noted not to imply minimality -- explicitly declining to validate either kernel candidate on this step's evidence.

rows.statement: The context map is sharpened: KnowledgeOS governs retrieval architecture and competes with none of it, deepening the R-2 mapping: governance (PAP) -> DP-n/capability (PDP) -> retrieval boundary (PEP). The industry's 'enforce before ranking' is the PEP placed exactly where R-7 already put it; KnowledgeOS is upstream policy, retrieval engines are downstream enforcement surfaces — a supplier relationship, not a rivalry.

rows.anchor: PM-6 (new): who retires KNOWLEDGE, as distinct from artifacts?
rows.statement: New question PM-6: who retires KNOWLEDGE, as distinct from artifacts? Checked before recording: artifact retirement machinery exists (superseded+superseded_by guard, archived by Knowledge Manager, historical standing, ADR-M 'Retired'), but retirement of KNOWLEDGE has never been observed in several registers, and no rule says when a RULE stops being true, only when a document does. PM-6's scope is enriched: the needed states (Candidate, Approved, Current, Deprecated, Historical, Retired, Superseded, Archived) are lifecycle states of KNOWLEDGE, not documents — this is MM-4's question (does state attach to the artifact or the rule it carries?) arriving from the retirement side. No machinery is designed; the question is sharpened, not answered.

rows.statement: A third validation stream, Lifecycle Validation, is recorded but not opened: it would validate transitions over time (whether the P-1..P-10 progression mechanisms occur as governed, at what rate, with what skips), since structure is validated (Stream 2) but time is not. rows.anchor: discovers · models · governs | individually EXERCISED and validated ... generates | n=0, inside and outside ... evolves | n≈3 informal ... guides product engineering | PARTIAL ... engineers software | OBSERVED ... collects evidence | OBSERVED ... improves KnowledgeOS | n≈3 informal

experiment.hypothesis: The composite R-6 chain (discover/model/govern/generate/evolve PKS via product engineering, engineer software, collect evidence, improve KnowledgeOS) is enacted end to end.
experiment.setup: Retrospective review of the corpus's own record of activity attributed to each named edge.
experiment.inputs: Rounds 16-31, WP deliveries (1,532 files), 106 evidence reports, CAP-001 section 9, OE-KOS-1 behavioural record
experiment.method: per-edge evidentiary grading
experiment.result: The loop's tail (engineer->evidence) is demonstrated; its head (generation) is not (n=0). The loop is broken at exactly one place: the generation edge.
experiment.interpretation: The uniqueness of the KnowledgeOS bet relocates to the generation edge and to the claim that one platform owns the whole governed lifecycle of product knowledge — no external instance found of this integration.
experiment.limitations: n=1 platform instance; 'guides product engineering' has no unguided baseline for comparison
experiment.conclusion: The narrow R-6 (generation) remains the first test; the composite is the full claim and requires both Stream 4 (generation) and Stage E (the loop) to prove — harder, not easier, than the narrow claim.

rows.anchor: What does OKF not prove — and why? ... the single blocker on the pipeline ... is NOT "nobody bothered." It is a gated entry point
rows.statement: OKF does not prove: that the feedback loop works (an article cannot prove this; the repository has the mechanism and zero traversals); that a knowledge layer improves engineering outcomes (no unguided baseline exists); that KnowledgeOS is a product (canon rules otherwise, AIP-14 Supporting Subdomain); that engineering knowledge behaves like enterprise knowledge (the article does not address engineering knowledge at all). The blocker on the feedback-loop pipeline is identified as a gated entry point, not apathy: ES-006.4's harvest question is asked at the retrospective, and the retrospective has not run — a concrete, dated, falsifiable blocker, more actionable than '0 traversals'.

rows.anchor: Lowest-confidence OKF insight applied to KnowledgeOS ... "The feedback loop completes the cycle." ... 0 traversals
rows.statement: The lowest-confidence OKF insight, 'the feedback loop completes the cycle', scores LOW: 0 traversals, the mechanism is governed in six places and has never executed once. The sharpened diagnosis: the loop's entry event, the retrospective, has not occurred — not apathy, an unfired trigger. This is the only OKF insight whose failure would invalidate the platform's central premise (that operational evidence becomes reusable engineering capability); everything else in the synthesis is corroboration, this one is load-bearing.

rows.anchor: Step 1 | Is the Knowledge Layer distinct from the Tool Layer, or conflated? ... there are TWO knowledge bodies
rows.statement: The Knowledge Layer is distinct from the Tool Layer in CAP-001 (Domain/Application are knowledge-free, Infrastructure reads knowledge), but a real conflation exists elsewhere: two knowledge bodies exist — the governed L-A corpus (in the graph, docs/knowledge/**) and the operational registers CAP-001 actually consumes (outside it, governed-registers.yaml) — no single 'Knowledge Layer' spans both.

rows.anchor: Category A — Independent Architectural Validation (A-1..A-12) — twelve conclusions, each derived twice by mutually blind paths
rows.statement: Twelve category-A validated conclusions with HIGH confidence, each doubly derived by mutually blind paths: A-1 KnowledgeOS is a governed hypothesis, gate shut; A-2 Product Primacy governs, 'laboratory' not canonical; A-3 the EKP is a real governed context with a named individual owner; A-4 Engineering Governance is the strongest bounded context; A-5 the reusable kernel (EEP, ES-001..006, Decision Model, Reference Architecture, Tactical DDD Principles, CAP-001 Domain/App/Shared, schema YAMLs minus bounded-contexts.yaml); A-6 designed-for-reuse != demonstrated-reusable, exactly one binding exists; A-7 Method (D-2/PD-2) is a distinct governed body via scope exclusion; A-8 three knowledge ontologies coexist unreconciled; A-9 enforcement lives runtime-side, capabilities are advisory; A-10 the invariant set; A-11 PMR-10's manual-adoption failure is operational evidence against protocol-only governance; A-12 the method itself is cross-validated (the blind reviewer prescribed the MVK experiment unaware it had run; predicted and actual measurements agree).
