rows.anchor: The six concepts ... MISSION · ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE · ENGINEERING CAPABILITY · ENGINEERING ARTIFACT · PRODUCT KNOWLEDGE SPACE · PRODUCT
rows.statement: Six concepts defined by responsibility/lifecycle/owner/dependencies, none defined by a folder: MISSION (why the platform exists; enacted->candidate->ratified, currently enacted-unratified; owner: sponsor; depends on nothing, the root); ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE (rules/methods/decisions that transfer between products; ES-006.1 ladder; owner DA for policy, sponsor+ARB for method; depends on MISSION); ENGINEERING CAPABILITY (protect exactly one invariant; observed->...->promoted; shape frozen under PGP-01..05; depends on MISSION+KNOWLEDGE); ENGINEERING ARTIFACT (carry knowledge in a representation, never the knowledge itself; statuses.yaml 8 states lint-enforced; owner field; depends on KNOWLEDGE); PRODUCT KNOWLEDGE SPACE (hold one product's concepts/language/contexts/bindings; authored today, generated as hypothesis n=0; owner product team; depends on KNOWLEDGE method + PRODUCT subject); PRODUCT (deliver business value; own delivery lifecycle; owner product team; depends on PKS + CAPABILITY).

rows.anchor: The model's most important edge — and why it matters ... ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE ≠ ENGINEERING ARTIFACT. One is the thing; the other is a carrier of it. This single distinction makes my recurring error UNSTATABLE
rows.statement: The Knowledge != Artifact edge makes a recurring three-times-repeated error class unstatable: claims like 'there is no strategic-DDD method', 'there is no capability pattern', 'the mission layer is vacant' become inexpressible, since under this model one can only say 'no artifact carries it', a representation claim, not a nature claim. A meta-model earns its place by making a known error class impossible to phrase; this one does. The reviewer's hierarchy is adopted: MISSION -> ENGINEERING CAPABILITY -> ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE -> ENGINEERING ARTIFACT (the lowest reusable layer) -> PKS -> PRODUCT; documents are the bottom of the model, not its centre.

rows.anchor: Q4 — which ontology elements exist BECAUSE they support a decision ... KNOWLEDGE ≠ ARTIFACT (I-1) | DetermineArtifactLifecycle | the deletion litmus … is UNASKABLE unless knowledge and its file are different things
rows.statement: Nine ontology elements are each bound to the specific decision they serve, applying Evans' test: KNOWLEDGE!=ARTIFACT (I-1) underwrites the deletion litmus of DetermineArtifactLifecycle (unaskable unless knowledge and file differ); AUTHORITY-SCOPE serves DetermineConcern/DeterminePlacement; GOVERNANCE-STATUS serves DeterminePromotionPath; NATURE:normative-force serves DetermineApplicableStandards; DP-n anchoring serves the approve-capability-change decision; CONTAINER boundary would serve the extraction/adoption decision (the MVK FAIL is this decision made without the model); PROJECTION+attestation (corrected I-4) serves the trust-or-rebuild decision; EVIDENCE-STATUS serves the earns/grants promotion gate; the four partial orders serve the direction-of-change-propagation decision.

rows.anchor: The kinds that emerge — four, plus one non-progression ... The mechanisms are NOT ten instances of "lifecycle." They are four different KINDS of change
rows.statement: Ten mechanisms reduce to four kinds of change plus one non-progression: GOVERNANCE-ACT progression (moved by a decision by a named role, reversible only by a further act; P-1, P-5, P-9); EVIDENTIAL progression (moved by accumulating evidence, nobody can decree it, reversible only by refutation; P-4, P-10); WORK-EXECUTION progression (moved by time and effort, has a clock, irreversible; P-7, P-8); COMPOSITE trajectory (crosses the above; P-3, P-6); and NON-PROGRESSION: PROVENANCE (moved by nothing, an immutable fact of origin, meaningless to reverse; half of P-2). The distinction that carries everything: a governance-act progression can be granted; an evidential progression can only be earned.

rows.anchor: Independence and interactions ... P-3 / P-6 consume P-10 ... evidence EARNS; governance GRANTS; promotion requires BOTH
rows.statement: Independence/interaction findings: status is orthogonal to authority (declared); ADR-status is orthogonal to maturity (declared); status depends on authority at one point via a guard (baseline requires authority in {authoritative, derived}) — coupling by guard, not fusion; P-3/P-6 consume P-10, stated as the platform's central mechanism: 'evidence EARNS; governance GRANTS; promotion requires BOTH'; P-7 produces P-10 (work produces evidence); P-1 vs P-5 are the same kind (governance-act workflow) applied to different artifact classes (a parsimony question, not an ontology question); P-3 vs P-4 are genuinely different kinds (composite-with-gate vs purely evidential).
invariants: evidence earns, governance grants, promotion requires both

rows.anchor: The success criterion — why multiple progression mechanisms exist ... A single unified lifecycle would force one engine onto all four
rows.statement: Multiple progression mechanisms exist because engineering knowledge changes in four causally different ways (governance position by acts per decision by named roles; evidential standing by evidence per occurrence, owned by nobody, earned; the work around it by time per session, owned by the executing team; its origin, which never changes) and the repository mostly deliberately refuses to conflate them. A single unified lifecycle would force one engine onto all four, requiring either that evidence be grantable by decree or that decisions wait on evidence that may never come; the repository's two declared orthogonalities and GEP-F1 are three prior refusals of exactly that fusion. No mechanism needs redesign on this evidence; what P-2 needs is separation of its two questions, which is an ARB decision.

rows.anchor: Part 5 — Lifecycle ... KnowledgeOS → creates PKS | HYPOTHESIZED, n=0 ... Evidence → improves KnowledgeOS | EMPTY, blocker: the retrospective has not run
rows.statement: Four commissioned lifecycle links graded: KnowledgeOS->creates PKS is hypothesized (n=0, PublicDigit's PKS was authored, not generated); PKS->guides Product is partially evidenced (protocol used, never measured against an unguided baseline); Product->generates Evidence is observed (106 verification reports, 1,532 code files); Evidence->improves KnowledgeOS is empty (blocker: the retrospective has not run). Two links inside the platform not in the commissioned chain are observed: Documentation Ontology->Knowledge Graph (knowledge-graph.php) and Documentation Ontology->Indexes (portal/INDEX.md, authority:derived). Only one of four commissioned links is observed; the loop-closing link is empty and the loop's first link has never run once — the cycle is the mission's hypothesis, not its description.
missing: evidence->platform improvement link for this product

rows.anchor: Invariant relationships vs implementation choices ... I-1..I-11 ... 11 invariants · 8 choices
rows.statement: Eleven invariants traced to governed statements: I-1 Knowledge is represented by an Artifact, an Artifact is never the Knowledge; I-2 a Capability protects exactly one invariant; I-3 a Knowledge Space has a declared boundary; I-4 (underspecified, not false — holds until attestation, reclassified as a lifecycle gap not an ontology falsification, per DP-2's conflation of derivation with attestation); I-5 one authoritative artifact per topic+context (lint-enforced); I-6 the Runtime never owns Knowledge; I-7 a PKS never contains reusable Method (stated and breached); I-8 governance precedes automation; I-9 governance-status orthogonal to authority; I-10 a constitutional principle is void-overriding; I-11 (restated 2026-08-02: Knowledge does not execute, capabilities execute, knowledge constrains and informs generation — the restatement survived cross-product projection where the original would have failed). Eight implementation choices (folder mapping, markdown as representation, YAML/Mermaid, the graph's declared scope, Claude Code as the n=1 runtime adapter, frontmatter, identifier formats, Mermaid+markdown projections) may change freely without breaking the model — that distinction is what makes this a platform rather than a repository layout.

lineage_claims.quote: KNOWLEDGE DOES NOT EXECUTE. Capabilities execute. Knowledge CONSTRAINS AND INFORMS generation.

rows.anchor: FOUR PRE-VALIDATION CORRECTIONS ACCEPTED — applied BEFORE the ontology was frozen
rows.statement: Four pre-validation corrections: (1) I-11 'Knowledge is never generative' is too strong, restated as 'Knowledge does not execute; Capabilities execute; Knowledge constrains and informs generation' — sharper and testable, and it survives projection where the original would not; (2) 'Engineering Method' may be a missing layer is recorded as hypothesis only, distinguished from Method already existing as domain PD-2; (3) Runtime Adapter belongs outside the core ontology is accepted and empirically confirmed by disappearing in all three projections; (4) the ontology models containment but not specialization is accepted as the single most consequential gap the projection confirms.

rows.anchor: VERDICT: FAIL — the MVK is insufficient to bootstrap a product ... SCOPE CORRECTION (PA, 2026-08-02) ... This FAIL invalidated the EXTRACTION BOUNDARY. It did NOT invalidate the platform
rows.statement: The bootstrap experiment's verdict is FAIL for the specific 15-file MVK extraction boundary, not for the platform generally: the engineering process (EEP transferred with zero translation; tactical principles rejected five candidates in a foreign domain) was validated. AR-1 (the risk of 'extracting a platform that cannot bootstrap', rated HIGH) is realized and caught before extraction, which is the experiment working, not failing.

rows.anchor: OE-KOS-1 · WP-4B delivery planning under the adopted architecture (2026-08-03) ... the first operational validation of the KnowledgeOS governance model in a real delivery planning activity
rows.statement: OE-KOS-1 records the platform's first observed real-work exercise since Phase V opened: a real delivery-planning activity (WP-4B) executed inside the adopted architecture. Observed behaviours: architecture constrained delivery planning (demonstrated); governance prevented unauthorized scope expansion (demonstrated — WP-4C/4D plans refused for lack of authorization); implementation questions stayed implementation questions (demonstrated); architecture preserved during planning (demonstrated). Not yet demonstrated: implementation completion, runtime behavior validation. This is the first recorded behavioural observation of the R-6 'guides PRODUCT ENGINEERING' edge working (still no unguided baseline); the back-edge (evidence->platform change) is explicitly NOT traversed by this entry.

rows.anchor: OE-KOS-2 · WP-4B RED-ratchet implementation slice (2026-08-03) ... K2 isolated as the slice's single behavioural invariant ... an honest stop at a clean boundary
rows.statement: OE-KOS-2 records a real implementation iteration (WP-4B RED-ratchet form): K2 isolated as the slice's single behavioural invariant with K1/K3/K4 reclassified as supports; 'no producer logic in the seam' named explicitly where current tests cannot detect its violation; implementation cost recorded before being paid; an honest stop at a clean boundary rather than falsely reporting green. This is a second formal behavioural record for R-6 (n=2): planning obeyed constraints in OE-KOS-1, implementation now obeys them under RED discipline. Still not the back-edge; no platform change occurred. The review proposes a candidate reusable kind, 'Implementation Finding' (IF-1), recorded at n=1, watch only.

rows.anchor: OE-KOS-3 · Developer-guide obligation skipped; safety-net blind spot found and fixed (2026-08-04) ... The gap was discovered by USER AUDIT, not by the platform ... THE BACK-EDGE, formally traversed for the first time — at the INSTRUMENTATION level
rows.statement: OE-KOS-3 records the Developer-Guide Definition of Done being skipped across every engineering-tooling step (zero guides written), and a Stop-hook safety net staying silent for a structural reason: its area-derivation pattern matched app/Contexts/, app/, database/migrations/ but not scripts/**, so changed files there produced zero code areas. The gap was found by user audit, not by the platform. Remediation same-turn: 4 guides written, the hook extended, fix verified twice. This is graded as the back-edge (evidence -> platform-machinery change) formally traversed for the first time, at the instrumentation level (n=1, instrumentation-level, distinct from the informal n≈3 for canon-level changes). DG-1 is recorded: the first counted instance is a failure-mode instance (implementation shipped without guidance while the net was also silent — the obligation binds regardless of reminders).

rows.anchor: OE-KOS-4 · WP-4C-2: discovery refused to invent a business decision (2026-08-04) ... a missing business decision, not a missing if-statement ... No RED plan was written
rows.statement: OE-KOS-4 records a discovery (WP-4C-2, Contestation) that gathered evidence and explicitly refused to answer the design question it uncovered — a missing business decision (an existing state transition requires a DeterminationId a failure event deliberately lacks), not a missing if-statement — kept the boundary in its own words, listed adjacent states without recommending one, and surfaced an unrequested adjacent finding without assuming both problems share an answer; no RED plan was written since that would encode an invented disposition. This is a third formal behavioural record for R-6 (n=3): planning obeyed constraints, RED implementation obeyed constraints, discovery refused to legislate — the process can now say 'we know enough to know implementation would be premature.'

rows.anchor: The two streams — and the check-before finding ... Stream B ... Pattern Cards (EPC-nnn) + the Pattern Evidence Register ... Stream B is that machinery finally receiving its input feed — nothing new is created
rows.statement: Two streams are distinguished: Stream A (Operational Evidence, what happened, append-only, this register) and Stream B (Learning Candidates, what recurring pattern appears, generated periodically from Stream A, reviewed by the DA, never written directly). Check-before finding: Stream B's home already exists — Pattern Cards (EPC-nnn) plus the Pattern Evidence Register (reserved namespace knowledge/evidence/, trigger 'PB-004 retrospective') — so the register's growth is what arms an existing trigger, nothing new is created. This prevents the register from slowly becoming another architecture document.

rows.anchor: Register annotations — OE-KOS-4 review dispositions ... R-6 scope check — PERFORMED, not assumed ... the count stands without stretching the edge
rows.statement: A check is performed (not assumed) on whether R-6's n=3 count is valid: the edge 'guides product engineering' is defined at the activity level, not the implementation level, in the Relationship Validation Matrix, and planning/implementation/discovery are all product-engineering activities, so the count stands; had R-6 been implementation-scoped, the count would have been trimmed to n=1.

rows.anchor: P4 · The Evidence Harvest — the loop-closing pattern ... NOT Evidence → Decision → Change. IS Evidence → HARVEST → Candidate → Promotion → Change
rows.statement: The evidence harvest pattern is corrected: not Evidence -> Decision -> Change, but Evidence -> HARVEST -> Candidate -> Promotion -> Change. The mechanisms (ES-006.4 harvest question, ES-006.1 ladder, Observation Protocol) are ready to use; Pattern Cards + Evidence Register are blocked on the PB-004 retrospective trigger; the CAP-001 evidence record has one row as of this document. The process exists; only the instances were missing, and one now exists.

rows.anchor: The register (24 deferred concepts with current invariant / activation criterion / evidence required / status)
rows.statement: A register of ~24 deferred architectural concepts, each with a current invariant protecting the need today, an explicit engineering-event activation criterion, required evidence, and a status (STAGED/PARKED/REJECTED FOR NOW/GATED/WATCHED/ACTIVE): DecisionCaptureService, Observation Runtime, Event bus, AssessmentPolicy, AssessmentEvidence, Pattern Register machinery, Evidence Analytics, Adaptive Recommendation, Recommendation/Decision/Outcome/Assessment bounded context, Bucket aging projection, Flow-efficiency refinement, Platform extraction, EIS rendering, MO-2 promotion, Engineering Assessment Commission, Real-Time ObservationTrigger adapter, Live decision capture, Incremental impact analysis, Telemetry enrichments (3 sub-items), FileSaved/IDE trigger, CI/PR trigger, Platform Bootstrap Track A (infrastructure automation), Platform Bootstrap Track B (reusable-platform extraction).

rows.anchor: Evidence Gaps — G-C1 THE EVOLUTION LOOP'S RETURN ARROW HAS NEVER BEEN TRAVERSED ... Three of the loop's four arrows are unevidenced, and the return arrow is empirically empty
rows.statement: A dependency graph of the platform's lifecycle loop shows: KnowledgeOS->generates->PKS is speculative (no PKS generated by it); PKS->guides->PublicDigit is speculative (asserted, not measured); PublicDigit->produces->Evidence is evidenced (106 verification reports); Evidence->improves->KnowledgeOS is empty ('ZERO-INDEPENDENT... never traversed', EAD-1). Three of four arrows are unevidenced and the return arrow is empirically empty — the loop is the accepted destination, not yet an observed cycle. Additional gaps: CAP-001 0 executions/0 decisions changed; zero market data points; no second adopting product; no second runtime adapter; six ES standards remain PROPOSED; H-CAT-1 refused the parent capability abstraction.

rows.anchor: The knowledge lifecycle — inferred, not invented ... Two stages exist here that the commission's example lifecycle omits — CHALLENGE and SATURATION
rows.statement: An inferred knowledge lifecycle: Discovery -> Assessment -> Challenge -> Saturation Gate -> Decision -> Governance -> Execution -> Evidence -> Harvest (ES-006.4) -> Promotion (ES-006.1) -> Platform. Two evidenced stages (Challenge and Saturation) are not in the commission's example lifecycle. The final arrow (harvest->promotion feeding the platform) has never been traversed.

rows.anchor: The process ... Engineering Reality → Observation → Recommendation → Decision → Outcome → Assessment → Learning (FUTURE)
rows.statement: A six/seven-stage process is described: Engineering Reality (collectors observe metrics/test presence/LCOM4) -> Observation (verdict-free) -> Recommendation (advisory, deterministic rules evaluate) -> Decision (a developer decides ACCEPTED/IGNORED/DEFERRED with rationale; IGNORED is a complete path, not a gap) -> Outcome (commits accumulate to >=MIN_COMMITS, a raw record, assessment-free) -> Assessment (a deterministic policy interprets: SUPPORTED/PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED/NOT_SUPPORTED/INCONCLUSIVE) -> Learning (FUTURE, consumes assessments never raw metric deltas, gated on evidence volume).

rows.anchor: Process rules (all pre-existing — this document restates, it does not legislate)
rows.statement: Four process rules, all pre-existing and merely restated: (1) every stage transition is a recorded event with timestamp and provenance; projections (funnel, lead times, Evidence Velocity, Loop Completion, effectiveness) are read-side interpretations that never write back; (2) recommendations are advisory, decisions belong to developers, a recommendation with no decision is meaningful operational data; (3) projections never infer missing data — sub-week windows withhold rates, INCONCLUSIVE is a first-class verdict, IGNORED is closure, not a gap; (4) the process is falsifiable end to end, able to show that a rule never helps, that recommendations go undecided, or that KnowledgeOS itself changes nothing.
invariants: recommendations are advisory; decisions belong to developers
every stage transition is a recorded event with provenance

rows.anchor: retrieved evidence does not automatically justify the inference you want to make.
rows.statement: Freedman is framed as improving RAG: the RAG pipeline (retrieve evidence) is extended to Evidence Retrieval -> Evidence Qualification -> Inference Construction -> Assumption Analysis -> Alternative Explanation Analysis -> Validation -> Claim.

rows.anchor: judgment is required to determine: Which question? Which data? Which assumptions? ... before causal inference, the right question needs to be framed, followed by identifying natural variation, collecting data, considering confounders and testing alternatives.
rows.statement: Connects this book to a prior 'Human-AI Interaction' book: that book said AI should not replace human judgment, and Freedman explains why -- judgment determines which question/data/assumptions/mechanism/confounders/alternatives/method/evidence and what a result establishes; the architecture should therefore start with Question -> Research framing -> Evidence -> Method -> Inference -> Challenge -> Validation -> Claim, not AI -> answer.

rows.anchor: Intervention: DO(X) ... OBSERVE -> HYPOTHESIZE -> INTERVENE -> OBSERVE OUTCOME -> UPDATE CAUSAL EVIDENCE ... KnowledgeOS becomes capable of supporting organizational learning, not merely document retrieval.
rows.statement: Intervention Lens: represent claims as do(X) interventions with expected outcome and counterfactual, enabling an OBSERVE->HYPOTHESIZE->INTERVENE->OBSERVE OUTCOME->UPDATE CAUSAL EVIDENCE loop that supports organizational learning rather than mere document retrieval.

lexical.anchor: Platform Lifecycle (Idea→Knowledge→PKS→Implementation→Evidence→Evolution) ... B-1 correction: software→evidence OBSERVED · back-edge n≈3 informal / ≈2 formal · KnowledgeOS→PKS n=0 · Genesis has NO route

conceptual.anchor: Knowledge Flow — four kinds of change + one non-progression; "evidence EARNS · governance GRANTS · promotion requires BOTH"

formal.anchor: The corrected canonical chain: MISSION (enacted) → STRATEGY → PRINCIPLE → DESIGN POLICY → CAPABILITY ...

rationale_evidence.anchor: Platform Lifecycle (Idea→Knowledge→PKS→Implementation→Evidence→Evolution) ... B-1 correction: software→evidence OBSERVED · back-edge n≈3 informal / ≈2 formal · KnowledgeOS→PKS n=0 · Genesis has NO route
rationale_evidence.statement: The platform lifecycle is graded link-by-link: software-to-evidence is observed; the back-edge is n≈3 informal / ≈2 formal; KnowledgeOS-to-PKS generation is n=0; and the Genesis stage has no route at all. Individual grades are confirmed; the loop as a whole remains a hypothesis.

rationale_evidence.anchor: KnowledgeOS —governs→ retrieval architecture (RAG · GraphRAG · KG · vector search) — and COMPETES WITH NONE OF IT
rationale_evidence.statement: The context map is sharpened: KnowledgeOS governs retrieval architecture and competes with none of it, deepening the R-2 mapping: governance (PAP) -> DP-n/capability (PDP) -> retrieval boundary (PEP). The industry's 'enforce before ranking' is the PEP placed exactly where R-7 already put it; KnowledgeOS is upstream policy, retrieval engines are downstream enforcement surfaces — a supplier relationship, not a rivalry.

rationale_evidence.anchor: discovers · models · governs | individually EXERCISED and validated ... generates | n=0, inside and outside ... evolves | n≈3 informal ... guides product engineering | PARTIAL ... engineers software | OBSERVED ... collects evidence | OBSERVED ... improves KnowledgeOS | n≈3 informal
rationale_evidence.statement: Each edge of the composite R-6 chain is graded individually: discovers/models/governs are individually exercised and validated (Rounds 16-31 executed; the method survived a foreign domain); generates is n=0 inside and outside; evolves is n≈3 informal (B-1's fact); guides-product-engineering is partial (protocol used, effect unmeasured, no unguided baseline) with a first formal behavioural record OE-KOS-1 (WP-4B delivery planning obeyed the architecture); engineers-software is observed (1,532 files, the WP deliveries); collects-evidence is observed (106 reports, CAP-001 section 9); improves-KnowledgeOS is n≈3 informal, the loop's back-edge, same fact as evolves seen from the platform side.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Concept relationships — the reviewer's example chain, validated ... KnowledgeOS creates PKS contains Engineering Knowledge organized by Ontology used by Capabilities executed through Runtime produces Evidence improves KnowledgeOS
rationale_evidence.statement: The proposed chain is validated edge by edge: 'KnowledgeOS creates PKS' is a hypothesis (n=0, every PKS is authored by a person); 'PKS contains Engineering Knowledge' is WRONG, violating I-7 (a PKS contains product knowledge and bindings; reusable method must not live in it — the current breach is the exception that proves the rule); 'knowledge organized by Ontology' holds with the precision that L-A organizes artifacts/carriers, not knowledge itself (I-1); 'used by Capabilities' holds (capabilities may read across space boundaries, never own — H-1); 'Capabilities executed through Runtime' is imprecise (capabilities are advisory scripts invoked on demand; the runtime executes Execution Assets/ASTs; 41 enforced controls live runtime-side while every capability is advisory — the drawn edge hides this finding); 'Runtime produces Evidence' should attribute production to WORK (P-7/P-8), the runtime only hosts the work; 'Evidence improves KnowledgeOS' is only partly true (n≈3 informal, B-1's fact).

rationale_evidence.anchor: What does OKF not prove — and why? ... the single blocker on the pipeline ... is NOT "nobody bothered." It is a gated entry point
rationale_evidence.statement: OKF does not prove: that the feedback loop works (an article cannot prove this; the repository has the mechanism and zero traversals); that a knowledge layer improves engineering outcomes (no unguided baseline exists); that KnowledgeOS is a product (canon rules otherwise, AIP-14 Supporting Subdomain); that engineering knowledge behaves like enterprise knowledge (the article does not address engineering knowledge at all). The blocker on the feedback-loop pipeline is identified as a gated entry point, not apathy: ES-006.4's harvest question is asked at the retrospective, and the retrospective has not run — a concrete, dated, falsifiable blocker, more actionable than '0 traversals'.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Step 1 | Is the Knowledge Layer distinct from the Tool Layer, or conflated? ... there are TWO knowledge bodies
rationale_evidence.statement: The Knowledge Layer is distinct from the Tool Layer in CAP-001 (Domain/Application are knowledge-free, Infrastructure reads knowledge), but a real conflation exists elsewhere: two knowledge bodies exist — the governed L-A corpus (in the graph, docs/knowledge/**) and the operational registers CAP-001 actually consumes (outside it, governed-registers.yaml) — no single 'Knowledge Layer' spans both.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The model's most important edge — and why it matters ... ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE ≠ ENGINEERING ARTIFACT. One is the thing; the other is a carrier of it. This single distinction makes my recurring error UNSTATABLE
rationale_evidence.statement: The Knowledge != Artifact edge makes a recurring three-times-repeated error class unstatable: claims like 'there is no strategic-DDD method', 'there is no capability pattern', 'the mission layer is vacant' become inexpressible, since under this model one can only say 'no artifact carries it', a representation claim, not a nature claim. A meta-model earns its place by making a known error class impossible to phrase; this one does. The reviewer's hierarchy is adopted: MISSION -> ENGINEERING CAPABILITY -> ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE -> ENGINEERING ARTIFACT (the lowest reusable layer) -> PKS -> PRODUCT; documents are the bottom of the model, not its centre.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Q4 — which ontology elements exist BECAUSE they support a decision ... KNOWLEDGE ≠ ARTIFACT (I-1) | DetermineArtifactLifecycle | the deletion litmus … is UNASKABLE unless knowledge and its file are different things
rationale_evidence.statement: Nine ontology elements are each bound to the specific decision they serve, applying Evans' test: KNOWLEDGE!=ARTIFACT (I-1) underwrites the deletion litmus of DetermineArtifactLifecycle (unaskable unless knowledge and file differ); AUTHORITY-SCOPE serves DetermineConcern/DeterminePlacement; GOVERNANCE-STATUS serves DeterminePromotionPath; NATURE:normative-force serves DetermineApplicableStandards; DP-n anchoring serves the approve-capability-change decision; CONTAINER boundary would serve the extraction/adoption decision (the MVK FAIL is this decision made without the model); PROJECTION+attestation (corrected I-4) serves the trust-or-rebuild decision; EVIDENCE-STATUS serves the earns/grants promotion gate; the four partial orders serve the direction-of-change-propagation decision.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The success criterion — why multiple progression mechanisms exist ... A single unified lifecycle would force one engine onto all four
rationale_evidence.statement: Multiple progression mechanisms exist because engineering knowledge changes in four causally different ways (governance position by acts per decision by named roles; evidential standing by evidence per occurrence, owned by nobody, earned; the work around it by time per session, owned by the executing team; its origin, which never changes) and the repository mostly deliberately refuses to conflate them. A single unified lifecycle would force one engine onto all four, requiring either that evidence be grantable by decree or that decisions wait on evidence that may never come; the repository's two declared orthogonalities and GEP-F1 are three prior refusals of exactly that fusion. No mechanism needs redesign on this evidence; what P-2 needs is separation of its two questions, which is an ARB decision.

rationale_evidence.anchor: retrieved evidence does not automatically justify the inference you want to make.
rationale_evidence.statement: Freedman is framed as improving RAG: the RAG pipeline (retrieve evidence) is extended to Evidence Retrieval -> Evidence Qualification -> Inference Construction -> Assumption Analysis -> Alternative Explanation Analysis -> Validation -> Claim.

rationale_evidence.anchor: judgment is required to determine: Which question? Which data? Which assumptions? ... before causal inference, the right question needs to be framed, followed by identifying natural variation, collecting data, considering confounders and testing alternatives.
rationale_evidence.statement: Connects this book to a prior 'Human-AI Interaction' book: that book said AI should not replace human judgment, and Freedman explains why -- judgment determines which question/data/assumptions/mechanism/confounders/alternatives/method/evidence and what a result establishes; the architecture should therefore start with Question -> Research framing -> Evidence -> Method -> Inference -> Challenge -> Validation -> Claim, not AI -> answer.

aliases: Causality, Counterfactuals, Interventions and Root-Cause Knowledge

sources.note: S0908's Step 25P: Pearl-style causal machinery (do-calculus, ATE, potential outcomes, identifiability) fully worked with falsification tests and DDD placement; extends B0021's causal-dependency-counterfactual-reasoning (S0870/Step 14) with root-cause analysis, necessary/sufficient causation, and integration into Sarathi's decision theory.

rows.anchor: TemporalPrecedence(A,B)\not\Rightarrow Causation(A,B) ... temporal ordering alone is insufficient
rows.statement: States the first theorem-like invariant: temporal precedence does not imply causation, illustrated with an upgrade-then-outage timeline that omits an intervening firewall change as an alternative cause.

rows.anchor: Sequence, Association, CausalHypothesis, CausalKnowledge ... increasing epistemic strength
rows.statement: Defines a four-level causal-knowledge hierarchy of increasing epistemic strength: Sequence (A≺B, directly observable ordering), Association (A~B, statistical association), CausalHypothesis (A=>?B, plausible provisional hypothesis), CausalKnowledge (A->B, accepted under an explicit causal model and evidence).

rows.anchor: CausalNarrative\neq CausalKnowledge ... an LLM ... The deployment caused the outage ... must represent CausalHypothesis rather than silently converting it to CausalFact
rows.statement: Warns that an LLM's narrative causal claim ('the deployment caused the outage') must be represented as CausalHypothesis, not silently converted to CausalFact — CausalNarrative ≠ CausalKnowledge.

rows.anchor: X_i=f_i(PA_i,U_i) ... Outage=f(Upgrade,FirewallChange,Load,UnknownFactors) ... genuine causal modeling rather than merely temporal reasoning
rows.statement: Introduces a structural causal model X_i=f_i(PA_i,U_i) (variable as function of causal parents and exogenous factors), worked as Outage=f(Upgrade,FirewallChange,Load,UnknownFactors) with an accompanying causal graph.

rows.anchor: G=(V,E) ... A\rightarrow B represents a causal hypothesis/model relation ... CausalGraph\neq ObservedWorld. It is a model of the world
rows.statement: Defines the causal graph G=(V,E) where an edge represents a causal hypothesis/model relation, not automatically empirical truth — CausalGraph ≠ ObservedWorld.

rows.anchor: Corr(X,Y)\neq0 ... IceCreamSales\uparrow and DrowningDeaths\uparrow ... Temperature\rightarrow both ... the classic confounding problem
rows.statement: The classic ice-cream/drowning/temperature confounding example: nonzero correlation does not establish causation since a common cause (temperature) may drive both variables.

rows.anchor: C\rightarrow A and C\rightarrow B ... A and B may appear associated even if A\nrightarrow B ... ConfounderCandidate ... especially important for root-cause analysis
rows.statement: Formalizes confounding (C->A and C->B can produce apparent A-B association absent direct causation), requiring KnowledgeOS to represent ConfounderCandidate, especially relevant for root-cause analysis.

rows.anchor: The earliest event before the failure is the root cause. That is wrong ... RootCause\neq EarliestPrecedingEvent
rows.statement: Rejects the naive 'earliest preceding event is the root cause' algorithm with a multi-step deployment/drift/firewall-change/outage timeline having several possible causal chains — RootCause ≠ EarliestPrecedingEvent.

rows.anchor: do(X=x) ... P(Y\mid do(X=x)) ... differs from P(Y\mid X=x) ... foundational to modern causal inference
rows.statement: Introduces Pearl's intervention operator do(X=x) and the distinction P(Y|do(X=x)) vs P(Y|X=x) — 'foundational to modern causal inference.'

rows.anchor: P(Outage\mid Upgrade)=0.2 ... does not necessarily mean P(Outage\mid do(Upgrade))=0.2 ... upgrades may occur precisely when systems already have problems
rows.statement: Worked example showing observational P(Outage|Upgrade) can diverge from interventional P(Outage|do(Upgrade)) because upgrades may be non-randomly timed relative to existing problems.

rows.anchor: does not always need interventions ... Observational evidence, Controlled experiment, Natural experiment, Simulation ... each should be explicitly typed
rows.statement: Notes causal reasoning does not always require real-world interventions, listing observational evidence, controlled experiment, natural experiment, and simulation as distinct, explicitly-typed evidence sources.

rows.anchor: CausalEvidenceType\in\{Observational,Experimental,QuasiExperimental,Simulation,StructuralModel,ExpertAssessment\} ... should not have identical evidential status
rows.statement: Defines a six-value CausalEvidenceType taxonomy, explicitly not carrying identical evidential status across types.

rows.anchor: ATE=E[Y\mid do(X=1)]-E[Y\mid do(X=0)] ... substantially stronger causal evidence than simple correlation ... even randomized experiments have assumptions and limitations
rows.statement: Defines the average treatment effect via random assignment, noting it is substantially stronger evidence than correlation but still carries assumptions/limitations.

rows.anchor: \tau=Y(1)-Y(0) ... Usually we cannot observe both simultaneously. This is the fundamental causal inference problem
rows.statement: Defines individual causal effect tau=Y(1)-Y(0) via potential outcomes, noting both cannot usually be jointly observed — 'the fundamental causal inference problem.'

rows.anchor: ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)] ... CausalEstimate: treatment/outcome/estimand/value/interval/model ... the model must be explicit
rows.statement: Defines ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)] as computable from appropriate designs, with a structured CausalEstimate record (treatment, outcome, estimand, value, interval, model) requiring an explicit model.

rows.anchor: Y_{do(X=0)} ... Y(0)=? ... generally not directly observable ... counterfactual conclusions require a model
rows.statement: Defines the counterfactual query (what would have happened under a different intervention, Y_do(X=0)), noting it is generally unobservable directly and requires a model.

rows.anchor: ObservedFact\neq Counterfactual ... Without the upgrade, the outage would not have happened must be typed as CounterfactualClaim ... should never silently enter the system as an observed fact
rows.statement: States the critical distinction ObservedFact ≠ Counterfactual: a counterfactual statement must be typed CounterfactualClaim and never silently enter as an observed fact.

rows.anchor: causal_confidence=0.93 unless the meaning is specified ... CausalAssessment=(Model,Assumptions,Data,Estimand,Estimate,Uncertainty)
rows.statement: Rejects a bare causal_confidence score, requiring a structured CausalAssessment=(Model,Assumptions,Data,Estimand,Estimate,Uncertainty).

rows.anchor: P(Y\mid do(X))=\sum_z P(Y\mid X,z)P(z) ... Identifiable=False ... this should become an explicit state
rows.statement: Introduces the identification concept: given sufficient adjustment variables Z, P(Y|do(X)) can sometimes be computed from observational data (backdoor-style formula) under appropriate causal assumptions; when no valid identification strategy exists, Identifiable=False must be an explicit state.

rows.anchor: If Identifiable=False, Sarathi should not manufacture a causal answer ... Zero=NeedCausalEvidence ... Lord can then determine whether experiment/observation/simulation/expert review could reduce the gap
rows.statement: States that non-identifiability feeds Zero=NeedCausalEvidence rather than a manufactured causal answer, letting Lord select experiment/additional observation/simulation/expert review as gap-reducing actions — 'fits our architecture beautifully.'

rows.anchor: G_1,G_2,G_3 ... if they produce different conclusions, causal knowledge is fragile ... CausalModelSet
rows.statement: Notes multiple plausible causal graphs (e.g. one implicating Upgrade, another Firewall) can yield model-dependent conclusions, requiring KnowledgeOS to preserve a CausalModelSet rather than a single graph.

rows.anchor: R=\{C_1,\ldots,C_n\} ... must not say C_i=RootCause merely because it has the highest score ... TopCandidate
rows.statement: Reformulates root-cause analysis as comparing a candidate set R={C1,...,Cn} by Support(Ci->Failure), explicitly forbidding declaring the highest-scoring candidate 'RootCause' merely by score — it is only 'TopCandidate.'

rows.anchor: RootCauseStatus\in\{Candidate,Supported,StronglySupported,Refuted,Undetermined,MultipleCauses\} ... much more realistic
rows.statement: Defines a six-value RootCauseStatus enum, 'much more realistic' than a single RootCause label.

rows.anchor: A\rightarrow B and C\rightarrow B ... A\land C\rightarrow B ... asking for one root cause is itself an incorrect model ... RootCause may be a set
rows.statement: Shows that when two causes jointly produce an effect (A∧C->B), demanding a single root cause is itself a modeling error — 'RootCause may be a set.'

rows.anchor: Necessary(A,B) versus Sufficient(A,B) ... necessary but not sufficient; sufficient but not necessary; both; neither
rows.statement: Distinguishes necessary causation (without A, B would not occur) from sufficient causation (whenever A occurs under the model, B occurs), with a four-way combination taxonomy.

rows.anchor: HighLoad\land ConfigurationError \rightarrow Outage ... neither alone is sufficient ... much closer to real engineering systems
rows.statement: Worked example: an outage requiring HighLoad AND ConfigurationError jointly, neither individually sufficient — 'much closer to real engineering systems.'

rows.anchor: CausalHypothesis, CausalAssessment, IncidentCauseAnalysis, Experiment ... Incident Management BC ... The generic KnowledgeOS layer provides epistemic infrastructure, while the bounded context defines what cause means operationally
rows.statement: Maps causal concepts onto DDD: rather than a generic 'Knowledge' aggregate, bounded-context-specific concepts (e.g. an Incident Management BC with Incident/Observation/CauseCandidate/CausalAssessment/RootCauseDecision) define what 'cause' means operationally, with the generic KnowledgeOS layer supplying epistemic infrastructure — 'a very important DDD boundary.'

rows.anchor: Observations->Variables->Causal Model->Identification->Analysis->Causal Assessment ... We observed A before B versus Our causal model estimates A caused B
rows.statement: Defines the causal provenance chain (Observations->Variables->Causal Model->Identification->Analysis->Causal Assessment), enabling the system to distinguish a bare temporal observation from a causal-model-derived conclusion.

rows.anchor: Simulation(Model,X)\rightarrow Y ... SimulatedOutcome ... SimulationEvidence\neq EmpiricalEvidence ... simulation can provide valuable evidence about consequences under a model
rows.statement: Defines simulation output as SimulatedOutcome, distinct from real-world observation — SimulationEvidence ≠ EmpiricalEvidence — while still valuable as evidence about model-implied consequences.

rows.anchor: World observation->Causal model->Simulation->Predicted outcome ... The prediction should not be treated as if the world actually produced it. This is especially important for Sarathi
rows.statement: Presents an epistemic chain from world observation through causal model and simulation to predicted outcome, warning the prediction must not be treated as an actual world-produced observation — flagged as especially important for Sarathi.

rows.anchor: P(Outage\mid do(Upgrade)) ... much more relevant than P(Outage\mid Upgrade) ... Sarathi is evaluating an action/intervention
rows.statement: Argues Sarathi's decision-relevant quantity is the interventional P(Outage|do(Upgrade)), not the observational P(Outage|Upgrade), since Sarathi evaluates an action/intervention.

rows.anchor: EU(do(X=x))=\sum_y P(y\mid do(X=x))U(y) ... CausalModel\rightarrow OutcomePrediction\rightarrow Utility\rightarrow Decision ... a major integration point between 25P and 25H
rows.statement: Formally integrates causal inference with decision theory: EU(do(X=x))=sum_y P(y|do(X=x))U(y), giving the chain CausalModel->OutcomePrediction->Utility->Decision — 'a major integration point between 25P and 25H.'

rows.anchor: if P(Y\mid do(X)) cannot be identified ... EU(do(X)) may not be reliably computable ... CausalIdentifiability becomes a prerequisite for certain quantitative decisions
rows.statement: States CausalIdentifiability as a prerequisite for reliable quantitative decision computation — an unidentifiable causal effect means EU(do(X)) may not be reliably computable.

rows.anchor: P(Outage\mid do(Upgrade))=0.05 versus =0.30 ... ModelUncertainty ... model averaging; bounds; sensitivity analysis; scenario analysis. But the chosen method must be explicit
rows.statement: Worked example of causal-model disagreement (two models yielding 0.05 vs 0.30) motivating explicit ModelUncertainty handling via model averaging, bounds, sensitivity analysis, or scenario analysis.

rows.anchor: P\in[0.05,0.30] ... Sarathi can determine whether the decision is robust ... DecisionFragility
rows.statement: Proposes representing causal uncertainty as an interval (P∈[0.05,0.30]) rather than a point estimate, letting Sarathi assess robustness — connecting directly to the earlier DecisionFragility concept.

rows.anchor: CK=(Cause,Effect,Model,Evidence,Identification,Assumptions,Estimate,Uncertainty,Validity)
rows.statement: Defines a consolidated nine-field CausalKnowledge tuple CK=(Cause,Effect,Model,Evidence,Identification,Assumptions,Estimate,Uncertainty,Validity).

rows.anchor: CausalAssertionType=\{Temporal,Associational,Hypothetical,Interventional,Counterfactual,Causal\} ... prevents semantic category errors
rows.statement: Defines a six-value CausalAssertionType taxonomy, preventing semantic category errors between temporal, associational, hypothetical, interventional, counterfactual, and causal claims.

rows.anchor: Falsification tests A-G: temporal ordering->Sequence not Causal; correlation->Association not Causation; controlled intervention->CausalEvidence; confounding structure->PotentialConfounding; unidentifiable effect->Unidentifiable; multiple sufficient causes->MultipleCauses; counterfactual question->C
rows.statement: Runs seven falsification tests (A-G, all PASS) against the causal model: temporal ordering alone yields Sequence, not automatically Causal; nonzero correlation yields Association, not automatically Causation; a controlled intervention (P(B|do(A))!=P(B|do(not A))) yields CausalEvidence (subject to experimental assumptions); a confounding structure yields PotentialConfounding; an unidentifiable causal effect yields CausalConclusion=Unidentifiable; jointly-required causes yield MultipleCauses; and a counterfactual question yields CounterfactualClaim, never ObservedFact.

experiment.hypothesis: The causal-knowledge hierarchy and its associated typing (Sequence/Association/Intervention/Confounding/Identifiability/MultipleCauses/Counterfactual) behave correctly across seven representative scenarios.
experiment.setup: Seven scenarios A-G spanning temporal ordering, correlation, controlled intervention, confounding, non-identifiability, multiple causes, and counterfactual reasoning.
experiment.inputs: n/a
experiment.method: apply the causal typing/classification rules to each scenario
experiment.result: All seven scenarios produce the theoretically expected classification
experiment.interpretation: Confirms the causal-knowledge model avoids collapsing temporal, associational, and causal claims into one category.
experiment.limitations: illustrative, not executed; intervention test explicitly noted as subject to experimental assumptions
experiment.conclusion: All seven tests PASS.

rows.anchor: graph traversal; d-separation; causal graph analysis; regression; Bayesian inference; simulation; counterfactual calculations ... No theoretical hardware barrier
rows.statement: Lists causal-graph operations (graph traversal, d-separation, causal graph analysis, regression, Bayesian inference, simulation, counterfactual calculations for specified models) as normal-PC computable; large Bayesian networks/Monte Carlo/large causal models may need more compute but 'no theoretical hardware barrier.'

rows.anchor: A computer can calculate P(Y\mid do(X)) given a valid causal model and appropriate data. It cannot prove that your causal model of reality is correct ... CausalComputation\neq CausalTruth ... mirrors our 25O result EpistemicAcceptance\neq WorldTruth
rows.statement: States the important limitation: causal inference depends on assumptions the computer cannot itself validate — CausalComputation ≠ CausalTruth, explicitly mirroring the 25O result EpistemicAcceptance ≠ WorldTruth.

lineage_claims.quote: This mirrors our 25O result: EpistemicAcceptance != WorldTruth.

rows.anchor: 25P — PASS ... Sequence, Association, CausalHypothesis, CausalAssessment, Intervention, Counterfactual, RootCause ... strength of causal conclusions depends fundamentally on CausalModel+Assumptions+Evidence
rows.statement: Step 25P self-verdict: PASS — the model computationally distinguishes Sequence, Association, CausalHypothesis, CausalAssessment, Intervention, Counterfactual, and RootCause, but conclusion strength always depends on CausalModel+Assumptions+Evidence.

rows.anchor: Evidence\rightarrow CausalModel\rightarrow OutcomePrediction\rightarrow Decision ... Sarathi can eventually reason not only what is true but what is likely to happen if we do X
rows.statement: States the major architectural result connecting Evidence->CausalModel->OutcomePrediction->Decision, letting Sarathi reason about action consequences ('what happens if we do X'), not only current truth.

rows.anchor: models themselves can be wrong ... How does KnowledgeOS represent competing models, compare them, select among them, and revise them when observations contradict predictions? ... Step 25Q
rows.statement: Closes by posing the model-fallibility question (models themselves can be wrong) and transitioning to Step 25Q (Models, Hypotheses, Prediction, Model Selection, Scientific Revision), with the central question of learning that a model is wrong without confusing model failure with evidence failure.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 25Q — Models, Hypotheses, Prediction, Model Selection and Scientific Revision

rows.anchor: How does KnowledgeOS reason about actions whose consequences are uncertain, irreversible, costly, or potentially dangerous? ... Knowledge->Decision->Intervention->World->Observation->Knowledge ... Prediction\neq Intervention ... P(Y|X) does not automatically tell us P(Y|do(X))
rows.statement: Closes by posing the action/intervention/control question and transitioning to Step 25Z (Action, Intervention, Control, Risk, Feedback), naming thirteen items to formalize (preconditions, authorization, expected utility, risk, reversibility, blast radius, intervention effects, feedback, monitoring, rollback, stopping conditions, human approval, safe failure) and introducing the key distinction Prediction ≠ Intervention.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 25Z — Action, Intervention, Control, Risk and Feedback

rows.anchor: X<->Y does not establish X->Y. KnowledgeOS must distinguish Association from Causation. This prevents another major AI reasoning error
rows.statement: Requires distinguishing association from causation as prevention of a major AI reasoning error.

rows.anchor: X->Y or Y->X or Z->X,Z->Y. Observational evidence may not distinguish them. Therefore CausalIdentifiability must be explicitly represented
rows.statement: Requires explicit representation of causal (graph) identifiability given observationally indistinguishable causal structures.

rows.statement: Defines root epistemic cause with three worked example root-cause categories.

sources.note: A corrective reformulation of R_req making it context/question-relative rather than a fixed universal set: R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq D (the distinctions required to answer question Q under context Gamma), Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq Preserved(R,Gamma), and Loss_req(pi,Q,Gamma) = R_req(Q,Gamma) intersect Collapsed(pi) as a required-information-loss metric (Loss_req=empty as the strong adequacy condition). Distilled into eight core propositions RREQ-1..RREQ-8 (Requiredness, Preservation, Collapse, Adequacy, Projection, Required Information Loss, Transformation Change, Reasoning-System Properties) proposed as the artifact KR-RREQ-2026-09, superseding a prior document's universal/literature-grounded R_req and its direct R_req->KernelSelection governance chain.

rows.anchor: I read the attached document in full. My assessment is that it is useful, but it is not yet safe to merge into the KnowledgeOS theory as written ... The most important work is therefore not to add all 10 proposed distinctions. It is to extract the valid theoretical contribution, correct the formalism, and prevent R_req from becoming an over-constraining 'master ontology.'
rows.statement: Executive verdict on an R_req/ratification-style document: classified as research analysis / candidate specification, not yet ratifiable; explicitly rejects the document's own recommendation to add all ten proposed distinctions and to ratify, warning against R_req becoming an over-constraining 'master ontology'; distills the strongest contribution as R_req = the distinctions that must remain available for KnowledgeOS's required questions, combined with Representation Adequacy iff required distinctions are preserved.

lineage_claims.target: an unnamed attached R_req document's ratification recommendation
lineage_claims.quote: I do not recommend following that recommendation directly

rows.anchor: the stronger KnowledgeOS definition should be: Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R preserves all distinctions in D_Q(Gamma) ... not: R preserves every distinction in D. The document itself notices this problem under projection adequacy, where it recommends allowing lower-tier distinctions to be lost. That observation should actually be moved up into the fundamental definition.
rows.statement: Corrects the pairwise-preservation definition of adequacy (d(x)!=d(y) implies R(x)!=R(y) for all d) to be question-relative from the start: Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R preserves all distinctions in D_Q(Gamma), not all distinctions in D universally -- because a representation may legitimately collapse a distinction irrelevant to the current question; promotes an observation the original document made only under 'projection adequacy' up into the foundational definition.

type_signature.domain: representation R, question Q, context Gamma

rows.anchor: For KnowledgeOS: Required != Interesting != Available in literature. A distinction belongs in R_req only if we can establish that some KnowledgeOS question, invariant, operation, assurance requirement or boundary requires it. ... analytic/synthetic, a priori/a posteriori, necessary/contingent, intentional/extensional, de dicto/de re ... their existence in the KR/philosophy literature does not establish that KnowledgeOS must preserve them.
rows.statement: States the principle Required != Interesting != Available-in-literature: a distinction enters R_req only if some KnowledgeOS question, invariant, operation, assurance requirement, or boundary can be shown to require it; existence in KR/philosophy literature alone (cited for analytic/synthetic, a priori/a posteriori, necessary/contingent, intensional/extensional, de dicto/de re) is not sufficient grounds.
invariants: literature presence alone does not establish requiredness

rows.anchor: A. Strong candidates: 1. Truth vs. validity ... 2. Satisfiability vs. unsatisfiability ... 3. Soundness vs. completeness ... 4. Decidability vs. undecidability ... 5. Local vs. global scope ... 6. Intensional vs. extensional ... 7. De dicto vs. de re ... B. Probably outside core R_req: Analytic vs. synthetic ... A priori vs. a posteriori ... Necessary vs. contingent ... These should remain external research candidates, not Tier 2 requirements.
rows.statement: Splits the document's ten proposed additional distinctions into Group A (strong candidates deserving further KnowledgeOS work: truth-vs-validity, satisfiability-vs-unsatisfiability, soundness-vs-completeness, decidability-vs-undecidability, local-vs-global scope, intensional-vs-extensional, de-dicto-vs-de-re) and Group B (probably outside core R_req: analytic-vs-synthetic, a-priori-vs-a-posteriori, necessary-vs-contingent), recommending Group B remain external research candidates rather than Tier 2 requirements.

rows.anchor: Truth vs. Validity -- |=alpha vs. Sigma|=alpha. This is not a clean distinction ... So the important distinction is: Validity != Entailment rather than: Truth != Validity. At the semantic level: M|=alpha is truth of alpha in a model M. Then |=alpha is validity across all models. And Sigma|=alpha is entailment from Sigma. This should be corrected before incorporating the item.
rows.statement: Corrects a formal error in the source document's Truth-vs-Validity distinction: the real three-way distinction is M|=alpha (truth of alpha in model M) versus |=alpha (validity: true in every model) versus Sigma|=alpha (entailment from Sigma); the document's proposed 'Truth vs Validity' pairing is not clean and should be replaced by Validity != Entailment before incorporation.

type_signature.domain: formula alpha, model M, theory Sigma

lineage_claims.quote: This is not a clean distinction

rows.anchor: we already have a critical KnowledgeOS boundary: Satisfiability != Contr because satisfiability is relative to Semantics + Language + ModelClass. Thus: Cons_S(K) iff exists M, M |=_S K could be a candidate formal consistency property. But it must not become: Contr(K) = not Cons_S(K). ... The attached document itself later says Contr requires Support Status and Resolution Status. That is actually evidence against identifying Contr with ordinary satisfiability.
rows.statement: Rejects identifying Contr with ordinary model-theoretic satisfiability: Satisfiability != Contr, since satisfiability is relative to Semantics+Language+ModelClass; proposes Cons_S(K) iff exists M: M|=_S K as a candidate formal consistency property distinct from Contr(K)=not-Cons_S(K), citing the source document's own admission that Contr requires Support Status and Resolution Status as evidence against the satisfiability identification, and listing Contr's broader required distinctions (genuine contradiction, incompatible contexts, temporal divergence, supersession, insufficient evidence, theory incompleteness).

type_signature.domain: knowledge base K under reasoning system S

missing: a full definition of Contr distinct from Cons_S

rows.anchor: soundness and completeness are properties of a reasoning system: Sound(S), Complete(S,Q). They are not properties of Knowledge itself. This should therefore be added under: Formal Representation and Reasoning rather than as a universal epistemic distinction. ... Decidability is a property of a problem/procedure/formal system ... Decidable(S,Q) ... Therefore: Decidability != EpistemicStatus. But it is extremely valuable as a reasoning-system capability/property. This fits our existing Complexity(S,Q) work.
rows.statement: Reclassifies Soundness (Sound(S)), Completeness (Complete(S,Q)), and Decidability (Decidable(S,Q)) as properties of the reasoning system S (a problem/procedure/formal-system property), not properties of Knowledge itself and not epistemic distinctions (Decidability != EpistemicStatus, distinct from Known(p) and Determined(p)); recommends filing them under 'Formal Representation and Reasoning' alongside an existing Complexity(S,Q) line of work rather than as universal epistemic distinctions in R_req.
invariants: Soundness/Completeness are properties of S, not of Knowledge

rows.anchor: The document identifies a weakness in its own preservation criterion: it does not account for context-sensitivity. This is correct. I would make the correction stronger. Instead of D_Q we should eventually have D_Q(Gamma) ... R_req may be a global baseline, while the actual required distinction set is: R_req(Q,Gamma). This is a major improvement.
rows.statement: Strengthens the source document's own context-sensitivity self-correction: replaces D_Q with D_Q(Gamma) where Gamma bundles context, scope, time, authority, task, and representation regime; correspondingly R_req becomes a global baseline while the actually-applicable set is R_req(Q,Gamma) -- described as a major theoretical improvement over a fixed universal set.

rows.anchor: I disagree with 'Tier 1 must always be preserved' ... A Tier-1 distinction d3 could be irrelevant to that question. Then R_1 may legitimately discard d3. So Tier(d) should influence governance priority, but should not automatically determine semantic preservation. The better rule is: Requiredness(Q,Gamma) > Tier.
rows.statement: Rejects the rule 'Tier 1 must always be preserved' as too rigid: even a Tier-1 distinction may be legitimately discarded by a representation used only for a task whose D_Q does not require it. Proposes Tier should govern governance priority, not automatically determine semantic preservation, i.e. Requiredness(Q,Gamma) takes precedence over Tier.
invariants: Requiredness(Q,Gamma) determines preservation, not Tier alone

lineage_claims.target: the source document's 'Tier 1 must always be preserved' rule
lineage_claims.quote: This is still too rigid

rows.anchor: The document says transformation invariance should preserve distinctions, but then recognizes that transformations may intentionally modify distinctions ... define a transformation's declared change set: Chg(T) subseteq R. Then: d not-in Chg(T) implies T must preserve d. This is much better for KnowledgeOS because some operations are supposed to change state. Otherwise the preservation requirement makes state transition impossible.
rows.statement: Corrects the transformation-invariance rule: instead of requiring T to preserve all of R_req, defines a declared change set Chg(T) subseteq R such that d not-in Chg(T) implies T must preserve d; explicitly noting that an unconditional preservation requirement would make state transition impossible, since some operations are supposed to change state.

type_signature.domain: transformation T and distinction set R
type_signature.codomain: Chg(T) subseteq R, plus a preservation obligation on R minus Chg(T)

invariants: d not-in Chg(T) implies T must preserve d

rows.anchor: The document says: delta must preserve all R_req distinctions. I would explicitly reject this formulation ... What must be preserved are the invariants declared applicable to that transition. So: InvariantCustody(delta) is preferable to: PreserveAll(delta, R_req). This aligns directly with our existing invariant-custody research.
rows.statement: Explicitly rejects the claim 'delta must preserve all R_req distinctions': a transition delta(K_t,a)->K_{t+1} may intentionally change status, support, currency, resolution, scope, even representation; proposes InvariantCustody(delta) -- preserving only the invariants declared applicable to that specific transition -- as preferable to PreserveAll(delta,R_req), aligned with existing invariant-custody research.

lineage_claims.target: the source document's claim that delta must preserve all R_req distinctions
lineage_claims.quote: I would explicitly reject this formulation

rows.anchor: 'Zero requires all Tier 1 distinctions' should NOT be adopted ... Zero does not necessarily need every distinction in R_req. Instead: Zero(K,I,Gamma,L) asks what is not justified by the available representation within the declared inquiry boundary. Therefore Zero's required distinctions are: R_Zero(I,Gamma,L) not automatically all Tier-1 distinctions. This is a major correction.
rows.statement: Rejects the claim 'Zero requires all Tier 1 distinctions': Zero(K,I,Gamma,L) does not need every R_req distinction, only R_Zero(I,Gamma,L), a distinct inquiry-relative subset; supports this by restating Zero's own existing epistemic-boundary vocabulary (Unknown!=Absent, NoEvidence!=EvidenceOfAbsence, Unresolved!=False, Representation!=Reality) as the actual grounding, rather than an automatic Tier-1 requirement.

type_signature.domain: inquiry I, context Gamma, lens L

invariants: Zero's required distinctions are R_Zero(I,Gamma,L), not automatically all Tier-1

lineage_claims.target: the source document's 'Zero requires all Tier 1 distinctions' claim
lineage_claims.quote: This is not established

rows.anchor: The 'minimality' definition is not yet mathematically sufficient ... minimal relative to what? ... the empty set R=empty could trivially satisfy many formal preservation conditions. The correct direction is something like: R_req(Q,Gamma) = minimal distinctions sufficient for all required questions Q, subject to declared adequacy criteria. This makes R_req task-grounded rather than literature-grounded.
rows.statement: Identifies a mathematical gap in the source document's minimality claim (a set claimed minimal 'relative to what?' -- as stated, an empty distinction set could trivially satisfy preservation/non-collapse/compositionality conditions); corrects the definition to R_req(Q,Gamma) = the minimal distinction set sufficient for all required questions Q, subject to declared adequacy criteria, making R_req task-grounded rather than literature-grounded.

rows.anchor: 'Completeness of R_req' is itself a dangerous concept ... There may be no useful universal set D_all. There can always be another task requiring another distinction. So instead of asking 'Is R_req complete?' we should ask: Complete relative to which task/question/domain? ... Complete(R_req,Q,Gamma) could mean: no currently declared required question in Q requires a distinction absent from R_req. That is a tractable governance question. 'Complete for all possible knowledge representation' is not.
rows.statement: Warns that asking whether R_req is 'complete' in an absolute sense is a dangerous, likely-unanswerable question (no useful universal distinction set D_all can be assumed to exist, since any new task can require a new distinction); replaces it with a tractable relativized governance question Complete(R_req,Q,Gamma): no currently declared required question in Q requires a distinction absent from R_req.

rows.anchor: The 47 distinctions should therefore NOT be frozen as universal ... Better: 47 currently identified candidate distinctions within the present KnowledgeOS research scope. ... We should preserve KnownSet(R) without claiming R=D.
rows.statement: Downgrades the source document's claim that its 47 distinctions form a comprehensive foundation, to '47 currently identified candidate distinctions within the present KnowledgeOS research scope', distinguishing the known distinction set KnownSet(R) from a claim that R equals the (unknowable) universal distinction set D.

lineage_claims.target: the source document's claim that 47 distinctions form a comprehensive foundation
lineage_claims.quote: I would downgrade this

rows.anchor: After filtering the document, I would extract seven concrete contributions. RQ-1 Required Distinction Set R_req(Q,Gamma) PROMOTE TO THEORY CANDIDATE ... RQ-2 Representation Preservation Preserve(R,d) PROMOTE ... RQ-3 Representation Collapse Collapse(R,d) PROMOTE ... RQ-4 Representation Adequacy Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) PROMOTE ... RQ-5 Contextual Requiredness R_req = f(Q,Gamma) PROMOTE ... RQ-6 Transformation Change Set Chg(T) subseteq R STRONG CANDIDATE ... RQ-7 Formal Reasoning Properties Sound(S), Complete(S,Q), Decidable(S,Q), Complexity(S,Q) PROMOTE AS REASONING-SYSTEM PROPERTIES
rows.statement: Lists seven concrete contributions extracted from the filtered document, each with a promotion status: RQ-1 Required Distinction Set R_req(Q,Gamma) (PROMOTE TO THEORY CANDIDATE); RQ-2 Preserve(R,d) (PROMOTE); RQ-3 Collapse(R,d) (PROMOTE); RQ-4 Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) (PROMOTE); RQ-5 Contextual Requiredness R_req=f(Q,Gamma) (PROMOTE); RQ-6 Transformation Change Set Chg(T) subseteq R (STRONG CANDIDATE); RQ-7 Formal Reasoning Properties Sound(S)/Complete(S,Q)/Decidable(S,Q)/Complexity(S,Q) (PROMOTE AS REASONING-SYSTEM PROPERTIES).

rows.anchor: Loss_req(pi,Q,Gamma) = R_req(Q,Gamma) intersect Collapsed(pi). Then: Loss_req = empty is a very strong adequacy condition. This is far more useful than a generic 'information loss' metric. ... FDE preserves some distinctions but collapses others. The relevant question is not 'Does FDE have four values?' It is: Does FDE preserve every distinction in R_req(Q,Gamma)? Our previous experiments already showed that it does not.
rows.statement: Defines Loss_req(pi,Q,Gamma) = R_req(Q,Gamma) intersect Collapsed(pi) as a required-information-loss metric, with Loss_req=empty as a strong adequacy condition, judged more useful than a generic information-loss measure; reframes the earlier FDE-insufficiency finding not as 'does FDE have four values' but as 'does FDE preserve every distinction in R_req(Q,Gamma)', concluding it does not (per prior experiments) -- positioning R_req as the formal language for STATING why a representation is inadequate rather than a prescription of which representation must be used.

type_signature.domain: projection pi, question Q, context Gamma
type_signature.codomain: a subset of R_req(Q,Gamma) that pi collapses

rows.anchor: Zero -> Boundary analysis -> Required distinctions rather than: Zero = absence of Tier-1 distinctions. This is a substantial theoretical improvement. ... each operation should have: Pre(delta), Post(delta), Inv(delta), Chg(delta). Then: d in Inv(delta) means the distinction must survive the transition. Whereas: d in Chg(delta) means the transition is explicitly permitted/required to change it. This is much more compatible with DDD and formal transition semantics.
rows.statement: Clarifies the role of Zero as Zero->Boundary-analysis->Required-distinctions (not Zero=absence-of-Tier-1-distinctions), and clarifies delta's structure as needing four named components -- Pre(delta), Post(delta), Inv(delta) (distinctions that must survive the transition), and Chg(delta) (distinctions the transition is permitted/required to change) -- judged more compatible with DDD and formal transition semantics than a single undifferentiated preserve-everything rule.
missing: formal definitions of Pre/Post/Inv/Chg for delta
invariants: d in Inv(delta) implies d must survive the transition
d in Chg(delta) implies the transition may/should change d

rows.anchor: The attached document recommends: HPA review -> feedback -> ratification -> kernel selection. I would change the last step. Do not: R_req -> KernelSelection directly. Instead: R_req -> AdequacyConstraints -> CandidateRepresentations -> CandidateOperations -> Verification -> KernelSelection. This is crucial. R_req tells us what must not be lost. It does not tell us which implementation/formalism is the kernel.
rows.statement: Rejects the source document's governance chain (HPA review -> feedback -> ratification -> kernel selection, with R_req feeding kernel selection directly), replacing the last step with a longer chain: R_req -> AdequacyConstraints -> CandidateRepresentations -> CandidateOperations -> Verification -> KernelSelection; states R_req tells us what must not be lost, not which implementation/formalism is the kernel.
invariants: R_req does not directly determine kernel selection

rows.anchor: Almost -- but not completely. As senior mathematician/statistician and DDD architect, I would say we have now closed one of the major structural holes in the KnowledgeOS theory, but we should not claim that the entire missing part is complete yet. The important distinction is: The missing theoretical layer is now substantially reconstructed; the remaining work is to prove/ratify its boundaries and connect it formally to the still-open operators.

rows.anchor: there are still four things we must NOT pretend are solved: A. R_req itself ... Framework complete != Set ratified. B. Evaluation semantics ... Eval_c is not closed yet. C. Zero / Contr ... R_req -> Zero/Contr is a useful connection, but not yet a definition. D. delta ... This is the largest remaining formal gap ... we still haven't established the actual delta signature, preconditions, postconditions, partiality and composition.
rows.statement: Names four things explicitly NOT solved despite the R_req reconstruction: (A) R_req itself -- the framework exists but the final authoritative ratified set does not (Framework complete != Set ratified; the 47 distinctions are a candidate corpus, not canonical ontology); (B) Evaluation semantics -- Eval_c(K,r,Gamma)->EVal has a better place to sit but is not closed (contradiction, insufficient evidence, theory incompleteness, temporal qualification, operational blockage, provenance insufficiency, status, boundary remain unresolved); (C) Zero/Contr -- R_req helps explain but does not define either, and Contr cannot become Contr=not-Cons_S(K); (D) delta -- the largest remaining formal gap, still lacking a signature, preconditions, postconditions, partiality, and composition rule.

rows.anchor: we still haven't established the actual signature, preconditions, postconditions, partiality and composition ... What is actually missing now ... (1) Required-distinction derivation ... (2) Evaluation domain ... including the distinction between U_epistemic and U_theory. (3) Determination semantics ... When does evaluation constitute determination? (4) Transition semantics ... Pre, Post, Inv, Chg, composition. (5) Equality / identity ... we know the four levels =, equiv, approx, cong_lambda but their operational roles remain unresolved. (6) Ratification ... the governance decision still has to ratify which propositions become theory.
rows.statement: Enumerates six precise remaining research items, framed as now-precise rather than vague: (1) how exactly R_req(Q,Gamma) is derived; (2) what exactly Eval_c can return, including the U_epistemic vs U_theory distinction; (3) when evaluation constitutes determination; (4) delta's full transition semantics (Pre, Post, Inv, Chg, composition); (5) the operational roles of the four known equality levels (=, equiv, approx, cong_lambda), still unresolved; (6) the outstanding governance ratification decision on which propositions become theory. Recommends the next step be internal synthesis/falsification rather than further literature accumulation (Literature extraction -> Candidate theory -> Cross-source reconciliation -> Formal tests -> Ratification, currently at the cross-source reconciliation/formalization stage).

rows.anchor: What the research has also confirmed: TRUE != BELIEVED != KNOWN, Explicit != Implicit, Stored != Derived != Entailed, Observed != Inferred != Reported, NoEvidence != NotAssessed, Unresolved != False, NoKnownGap != Complete, Representation != Reality. rows.statement: Notes that the reviewed report consolidates eight distinctions already independently discovered elsewhere in the KnowledgeOS research program (TRUE!=BELIEVED!=KNOWN, Explicit!=Implicit, Stored!=Derived!=Entailed, Observed!=Inferred!=Reported, NoEvidence!=NotAssessed, Unresolved!=False, NoKnownGap!=Complete, Representation!=Reality) as Tier-1 corpus distinctions, positioning R_req as a unifying framework rather than an isolated new idea.

rows.anchor: The proposed '10 additional distinctions' are NOT automatically part of the theory ... 'found in formal literature' does not imply 'required by KnowledgeOS' ... rows.statement: Reaffirms (independently of S2570 in this same batch) that ten literature-sourced distinctions proposed by the reviewed report are not automatically KnowledgeOS requirements, splitting them the same way into strong candidates (truth!=validity, satisfiability!=entailment, soundness!=completeness, decidability!=undecidability, local!=global, intensional!=extensional, de-dicto!=de-re) and likely-external ones (analytic/synthetic, a priori/a posteriori, necessary/contingent, rigid/non-rigid); states the correct pipeline as Literature distinction -> KnowledgeOS question -> requiredness test -> R_req, not a direct literature-to-primitive promotion.

rows.anchor: The five verification criteria are not yet final: 1. Distinction Preservation 2. Transformation Invariance 3. Projection Adequacy 4. Composition Preservation 5. Zero Compliance ... rows.statement: Reviews the report's five proposed verification criteria (Distinction Preservation, Transformation Invariance, Composition Preservation, Projection Adequacy, Zero Compliance) and rejects the same two over-strong instances S2570 rejects: 'delta/transformations preserve everything' (corrected to Chg(T) subseteq D with preservation required only outside Chg(T)) and 'Tier 1 must always be preserved' / 'Zero requires all Tier-1 distinctions' (corrected to R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq Preserved(pi) for the actual task, and a Zero-specific R_Zero(I,Gamma,L) rather than an automatic Tier-1 requirement).

rows.anchor: The completeness proof is still missing ... We probably do not want to prove that there exists one universal complete set of distinctions. A better target is R_req(Q,Gamma) being minimal and sufficient for a declared question/task family. Thus the real completeness question becomes: for all Q in Q_set, Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma), rather than: R_req = all distinctions that could ever exist.
rows.statement: Independently converges with S2570's completeness-reframing: rather than proving R_req is a universally complete distinction set, the defensible completeness target is R_req(Q,Gamma) minimal-and-sufficient for a declared question/task family, with the real completeness question being 'for all Q in a declared task family, does Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) hold' rather than 'does R_req equal all distinctions that could ever exist'.

rows.anchor: The document says: 'R_req is the non-negotiable subset of distinctions required by the system kernel.' That is circular. So the final formulation should be: R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq D and then Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq Preserved(R,Gamma). Status: CLOSED as foundational framework, after this wording correction.
rows.statement: Identifies a circularity in SPEC-R-REQ-2026-v1.0's own wording ('the non-negotiable subset of distinctions required by the system kernel' presupposes a kernel that has not yet been selected); corrects it back to the question/context-relative formulation R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq D with Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R_req(Q,Gamma) subseteq Preserved(R,Gamma); with this correction, R_req is judged CLOSED as a foundational framework.

formal.anchor: The document says transformation invariance should preserve distinctions, but then recognizes that transformations may intentionally modify distinctions ... define a transformation's declared change set: Chg(T) subseteq R. Then: d not-in Chg(T) implies T must preserve d. This is much better for KnowledgeOS because some operations are supposed to change state. Otherwise the preservation requirement makes state transition impossible.

governance.anchor: The attached document recommends: HPA review -> feedback -> ratification -> kernel selection. I would change the last step. Do not: R_req -> KernelSelection directly. Instead: R_req -> AdequacyConstraints -> CandidateRepresentations -> CandidateOperations -> Verification -> KernelSelection. This is crucial. R_req tells us what must not be lost. It does not tell us which implementation/formalism is the kernel.
